utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may begin, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the speakers please observe a pause between the questions an answers for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you both hear that? When you speak the same language there is that tendency, so, please, in the interest the interpretation observe the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will. Thank you, Your Honour. With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show the witness his statement, and I'm also going to send a binder of exhibits along with it. Your Honours should have before you a copy of the statement as well as the binder of the exhibits. The Defence has it as well, and so does the legal officer. To save time, we're going to do this the old physician fashioned way, Your Honours, with the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At times, it's more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, but it is a one time treat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, could you look at your statement, is this your statement and is it true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise this as the statement I made, and it is an accurate description of what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you were to testify today and the questions put -- were put you that relate to the topics in your statement, would you give the same answers as reflected in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this statement be admitted into evidence. It's 65 ter 3027.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 3, you state that on the 23rd of January, 1995, you took command of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where was your headquarters located?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The headquarters was in Sarajevo in a building called the Residency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what kind of reporting you received in your position as the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The formal reporting occurred with the support of my immediate staff in the headquarters. I should point out that the headquarters wasn't purely military. There was a political element within it; Political Affairs of the United Nations Department. The -- I was briefed every morning, I recall, at about 9.00 every morning. At this briefing, the events of the previous 24 hours were gone through, and everybody who was interested, as it were, was there around the table. It wasn't only my immediate staff, but there were people from UNHCR, ICRC, and other agencies present in Sarajevo at the time. Various decisions and so forth might be taken as a result of that briefing. There was a second formal event that occurred every day at about, again, my memory was it was about 5.00 in the afternoon, when a rather smaller gathering, essentially the headquarters rather than anybody from outside. We went through the events of the day so far, and I took -- I got briefings on matters that had arisen in the previous briefing in the morning or other more long-term inquires. And various decisions I might have had to make would be briefed to me at that particular time; and then over and above that, there was -- if it was urgent or something else, people would communicate with me straight away. In addition, I visited my sector headquarters as frequently as I could; and being in Sarajevo, the one that I visited the most would be Sector Sarajevo. So I saw a great deal of them. I was also in contact with the Federation and Bosnian governments and their officials, sometimes at a presidential level that. That gave me a source of information and reporting about what was going on, and, again, I heard from the Serb side when visiting Pale or through their liaison officer at Lukavica, so I get information from their point of view. And, lastly, there was a large journalistic gathering in which there was an interchange of information and so forth at that -- as that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you received information from the Serb liaison from Lukavica. Do you recall that person's name?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It -- Colonel Indic was the liaison officer. I think he was a colonel. He may have been a major but I can't -- let's call him a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to assess Colonel or Major Indic's relationship to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: My understanding is that he was General Mladic's liaison officer, a direct link to Mladic, and that's how he was dealt with. That is what he was there for, and how we worked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how you received information. I want to ask you a couple of questions about what kinds of information you received and focussing in particular on the warring parties in and around Sarajevo. Was it important to you in your position to receive information about and to assess the nature of -- the command and control of the two parties; that is, the Federation party or the Bosnian Muslim side and the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I had to understand how they were organised and operating, partly so I knew who to talk to, and partly so I could interpret what was happening in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it important for to you receive information about and to assess the strategy of the two factions in -- in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Indeed. Again, the reason for that is simply to be able to understand and, in this case, to be rather more predictive about what your looking at or what you anticipate would occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 16 of your statement, you stake about Mr. Karadzic and his political authority over the Bosnian Serbs. And in paragraph 21, you talk about General Mladic and his command over the Bosnian Serb army. I want to ask you a couple of questions about General Mladic. From your information and your observations, did General Mladic's command reach down to the level of the Bosnian Serb army around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. He was the overall commander, and he was evidently in command. He -- and his -- his influence could be felt at a very low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to give any specific examples briefly of that? How were you able to draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: This one isn't specific, just the general atmosphere with something. He said something was going to happen, it did. If you asked that something should stop happening and he said it would stop, it stopped. And a specific example isn't sanity around Sarajevo; but on one occasion driving towards Srebrenica, my vehicles got lost and we finished up in a very -- in a fairly -- a company position somewhere to the north of, I think, Velasnica [phoen]. It took one telephone call by my liaison officer to -- directly to Mladic to have us released. It was that -- he was able to be reached on that basis that quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, unless you're going to relate this ultimately to the general who is on trial, I don't immediately see its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the argument we're going to make is that if the command - and I'm about to elicit information about this - but the command is running from Mladic down to the ground in Sarajevo, the general is in that chain of command and so we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General Milosevic is that that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General Smith, the story that you just recounted is that in paragraph 31 of your statement? Is that --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you had discussions with General Mladic, did he have a familiarity or not with events that were occurring in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: He always knew what he was talking about, yes. So if it was an incident that was occurring about Srebrenica or he was raising it, he was certainly aware of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you just briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, didn't you earlier say that you didn't have an example of General Mladic's influence in relation to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't think of one immediately. The one that came to mind was this telephone when we were lost and arrested by this company position. I dare say if we go through all these paragraphs, I could find you one. Oh, I could give you one. There was an incident, if I recall, in March, when a -- two young girls on the Serb side were killed by sniper fire from the Bosnian side, and this -- I was -- it was a source of much discussion between General Mladic and me. And he knew the details of the case extremely well. Or the occasion when one of my soldiers was killed, a French soldier, by a sniper from the Serb side. Again, he was aware of the incident, knew the facts, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the manner in which General Mladic exercised his command? What was his style?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In short, he gave orders rather than missions. Now, to explain that a little, if you would like me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The -- in broad terms, there's two ways of running an organisation like an army. You can decentralize the decision, in which case you -- give missions, which I define as telling someone the result you want to achieved. For example, get my brigade over that river by lunchtime tomorrow. And you're not telling him whether he is to build a bridge or raft it across or capture a bridge or find a fort or whatever. You are leaving the manner of the doing entirely the individual on the ground on the spot. If, on the other hand, you centralise decisions, then you tend to give orders, which are much more specific, much more restraining, and then you would be-- you would give -- you would express -- take my example of crossing a river. Build me a bridge at X, Y, Z by such and such a time, and so on and so forth; and then you have to give someone else orders about what route management down to it. And someone else orders about who did traffic control and who did car parking and all the other things. All of which would be expected to be part of the other man's mission and him to work out how did he that. For very good reasons, Mladic ran his army on a centralised orders-based system. Is that enough of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is. Thank you. Based on the information that you received and your observations and your dealings with General Mladic and others, including Major Indic, were you able to determine whether General Mladic respected the chain of command in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He respected it in the sense that he used it in the way that I described. People beneath him were responsible for achieving the orders that he had given them and so forth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would he tolerate any breakdown in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Not that I observed, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at the first tab. It's 65 ter 2209. It's an order dated the 23rd of January, 1995, from General Mladic.?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we go back to the answer that the General gave to your question as to whether he would tolerate any breakdown in the chain of command, and you said, General, "not that I observed." Does that mean that you are not really able to answer that question, definitively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't in his army, so -- nor was I in his headquarters, so I wasn't able to see everything. What I observed is that he ran a tight ship, if I could use that phrase, and he was not a man that appeared to me to tolerate anyone not doing what he wanted them to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any -- any example of that of where there might have been a breach in the command and he set it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would put it the other way around. I saw no evidence that he wasn't expecting everyone to do what there were told as he told it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can put it no higher than that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, General Smith, please, I fully understood what you said about the command system of General Mladic, based on very specific orders and not on assigning a mission, which means that he could not tolerate any breach in the orders that had been given. In such a system, in such a command system, how much autonomy do inferiors have? People that are below the commander give -- get specific orders that they have to carry out, and they don't get missions. But if they don't obey the orders, according what you said, it seems like there is sanctions. So in General Mladic's system, the lower echelons, did they have any room for manoeuvre or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I understood and observed what I was looking at, and the -- I gave you the two extremes of the theoretical model, the orders based and the mission based. Of course, no system, no army fits precisely one or other extreme. It's -- things vary between those, and they vary not -- not only completely within the army as a whole, but at different levels in the army. And it often a reflection of the trust and confidence that the superior has in the subordinate. The way General Mladic was working, as I observed it, was that he was -- he would give his orders. He was able to, and this is part of his organization and system, create a forward headquarters from his main headquarters, and put an assistant commander or one of his senior staff officers forward to act in his name. And this allowed variations on the given order as events occurred, because he had his own man with the communications forward alongside the particular problem. And he did this quite a lot, particularly when he was engaged on some matter to the east of Republika Srpska, and there was a problem in the west, or vice versa. The degree of autonomy given in the order to carry out the order can be considerable. For -- let's go back to my building the bridge. That -- that engineer told to build the bridge would have complete freedom of action in the building of the bridge. But he would be expected to have built a bridge even if, actually, he had gone three miles down the river he could have found a ford, because his orders were to build a bridge. Have I explained enough the amount of the flexibility he has within that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, during your attention to the first document, 2209, is this order consistent or not consistent with the style of command that you have been explaining to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's -- it's really very detailed for something going down from an army headquarters to a corps headquarters, specifying the nature of the reports and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next exhibit, please, 65 ter 89, and turn specifically to the second page of the English. This is an order dated the 8th of March, 1995, from Mr. Karadzic. Is -- General, is this consistent with the authority and command of Mr. Karadzic that you describe in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. Here is the political direction, if you like, emanating from the Supreme command and, again, going into considerable detail and being passed down, I see from the cover letter, directly to the corps from the army headquarters. I think that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just checking. The first one was an order by whom? Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And this is now an order by Mr. Karadzic, and he speaks about Mr. Karadzic in his statement and his political authority and his authority over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the command system that he described would have related to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. And that is in -- the next exhibit will tie this into that, because Mr. Karadzic was of course the political leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The political leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Above -- I mean, he is the political leader giving commands down to Mr. Mladic, which then get translated down, and we will see an example of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next document, which is P -- I'm sorry, 65 ter 2267. The previous order from Mr. Karadzic was 8th of March, 1995. This is now an order from Mr. Mladic, General Mladic, on the 31st of March, 1995, entitled, "Directive for further operations, operative number 7/1." General, is this consistent with what you describe in terms of the relationship between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic and Mr. Mladic's command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I am just checking. It's a direct follow on, I think, from the previous one. He picks up the directive from the Supreme Command, and it's now being regurgitated in greater detail yet by the Main Staff of the army headquarters under Mladic's name. And the orders are going out to the corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Whiting, you speak of the consistency between this command and the description given by the General of the relationship between Karadzic and Mladic. Has he given such a description?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in his statement. I made reference to it in his statement. In paragraph 16, he talks about Mr. Karadzic; and in paragraph 21, he talks about Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're referring to paragraph 16 and 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I did refer to those earlier. And in paragraph 16, in the middle of the paragraph, he says, "In all my dealings with Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership, it was clear that Karadzic without doubt the leader of the Bosnian Serbs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him explain it. The evidence coming from him should be as self-contained as possible, as it is consistent with the economy that we wish to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm always trying to strike the balance and not try to repeat too much. It is in the statement, but I am happy to have him the General explain briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, how do you understood the relationship to be between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In, brief, Karadzic was the political, and evidently the political, leader of the Bosnian Serbs, and Mladic was the army commander. And they -- the distinction between the two was maintained in their -- in what they did and how they approached me and issues we dealt with. As the events of the year 1995, which is when I was there, went on and the pressure came on, the -- Mladic continued to maintain that he was the military commander. In practice at the level you're operating at, your military acts are directly political and to some extent vice versa if you're in the Karadzic position. So there is not as much -- as you might claim, there a is a clear line, in reality it's a fairly fuzzy line. But Mladic always held himself on to that military side as much as he possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P337, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, I want to ask you about the strategy of the two sides. By March of 1995, did you have a view about the attitude of the two factions towards the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, which I will refer to as COHA.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't know the paragraphs in this statement, but perhaps you could help me, but I cover it there. But in brief, I came -- I formed what I called a thesis as a basis on which to understand and interpret events that was before me. The essence of it was that neither side wanted peace at this point; this is March 1995. Evidently the COHA was breaking down in front of me. The Federation and the Bosnian government had been compressed into a relatively small area and had a -- had man power, as it were surplus and were in a position to attack. Their problem was a shortage of munitions and weapons. They also had the belief that they had the moral position and support, potential support, of the international community. So they were interested in breaking the siege of Sarajevo and advancing their position, as it were, by force of arms. The Bosnian Serbs had taken so much territory and had so few people in comparison that they were not in a position to expand their territory and hold it, and they were, as it were, at a limit. And the -- they had -- one of their biggest problems were the eastern enclaves; Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. From their point of view, these enclaves lay in their rear. And the Bosnians could operate out of them and were, and this required a proportion of manpower that they could ill afford to guard these enclaves, to secure these enclaves. So it was going to be it in their interest, I deduced, to do what I call squeezing the enclaves, which included squeezing the UN forces, so as to make them the very least problem and requiring the very least amount of guarding. And, indeed, this was already happening to us. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, I'm just going to interrupt for a moment. When you say "squeezing the enclaves," does that include Sarajevo or are you only talking --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I'm coming to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the witness is giving evidence under the abbreviated procedure, 92 ter. I should say that the Trial Chamber did consider whether it was the best way to receive his evidence, because it is important evidence to understand command responsibility. We, nonetheless, decided to accede to your application, but I see now that it may not be entirely appropriate to receive his evidence in this abbreviated way. And my instruction to you is, not withstanding 92 ter, you should feel free to adduce from the witness as much evidence as is needed to make it intelligible, understandable by the Chamber in the interest of the fairness of the trial. Do you understand? So you can take a little more time than I had given you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was hoping to finish the General's testimony today, because the General was hoping to be completed with this testimony today. I don't know what his ability is to be here tomorrow, and so we're trying to get it completed today. His statement is extremely detailed and so to kind of go over it again would take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. You don't have to go over it again, but I just say extract from him as much evidence as is needed to make our understanding of the command responsibility situation as complete as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I'll take that in mind. If I'm -- if, of course, it's not intelligible, I would invite, of course, not that I need to, but questions from Your Honours to clarify matters. But, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, General, you were about to get to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Sarajevo itself was an enclave, and I'm treating it separately because of its significant. In my thesis, I understood it to be the capital. It is the centre of attention of the international community, and the -- and the -- my expectation of -- and understanding of the Bosnian Serb strategy was to put the greatest possible pressure on Sarajevo and to have maintain the siege as tightly as they could. As a result, I expected them to try and close what was called the Igman trail, which was the one route that the Bosnian Serb army still had to get supplies and people into and out of Sarajevo through the tunnel that was under the airport. Equally I expected the Bosnian government to seek to hold Sarajevo very tightly and to try and lift the siege as quickly as they could. I haven't discussed the western -- north western enclave of Bihac, which was a rather separate set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll leave that for now. As the -- was there any relationship between the COHA breaking down on the one hand, and the siege of Sarajevo on the on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: As the COHA broke down and the breaking down was initiated by the Bosnian side, the siege of -- of Sarajevo became tighter and tighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb army use shelling and sniping of Sarajevo in any way?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there shelling and sniping of civilian areas, civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say "both," you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shelling and sniping in civilian areas and of civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to assess the strategy of the Bosnian Serb army using shelling and sniping of civilian areas in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: With the exception of countering a specific attack or something like that, the -- my understanding was that the use of these weapons were essentially to terrorise, to wear down the resolve of the defender, to hold the presence of the Serb pressure evidently in the minds of people on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it effective?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The -- it most certainly was and particularly on the ordinary run of life within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did it have any effect on the international community that was located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It considerably constrained, or rather, restrained our activities, and, as I've said, there were occasions when there was a direct effect; like we had a soldier killed or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some specific paragraphs in your statement. If we could look at paragraph 29 on page 7?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you're describing a meeting that you had with General Mladic on the 5th of March, and in paragraph 29 you said: "He threatened a complete blockade of all enclaves including Sarajevo if sanctions were not lifted." Did you take that threat seriously?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In that he could have done that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I'm just trying to look at -- this is when I'm at Jahorina. Yes. I did take it seriously. Again, at this point, I'm forming that thesis that I discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just to make sure I understand your answer, in your view, he had the ability to do that, to do what he threatened, with respect to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, demonstrably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next document, please, which is 65 ter 8. It's a --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- memorandum dated the 6th of March, 1995. It's about the meeting that you describe in your statement on the 5th of March, 1995. Have you had an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it an accurate account of your meeting with General Mladic on that date?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there anything of significance in the meeting that we should hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just covered a point that it was raised in the meeting, that General Mladic threatened a complete blockade of all of the enclaves. This meeting is described in detail in his statement, and this is a contemporaneous document which describes it. And on page 2 of the document, point 4, the end of the paragraph is where it says -- it says that he threatened a complete blockade of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I see that. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 of your statement, you describe being on the 12th of March arriving into Sarajevo by aeroplane and being hit by heavy machine-gun fire, and subsequent investigations proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the source of the fire was Bosnian Serb positions. Do you recall how that conclusion was reached?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't think there was any great difficulty, and I think, my memory is that -- it was acknowledged by the Bosnian Serbs that it was them who fired it. The Muslim side did not have that calibre of weapon. The firing came from a particular position on a small hill that overlooked the -- over the -- the Bosnian Serb position, overlooked the runway. And my -- what I recall that Mladic and co., when faces with this, acknowledge this it had been their people who had fired at the run.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 44 of your statement, please. And here you describe a meeting that you had with Dr. Karadzic on the 5th of April, 1995 in Pale. Do you recall this meeting and could you briefly tell us the significance of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: As I recall the meeting, we'd -- Mladic and I were not talking at this stage. I'm trying to remember why, and I can't immediately. It's probably in -- in one of these paragraphs here. But we certainly weren't talking to each other, and so I contacted Dr. Karadzic and we arranged to meet. My reasoning for wanting to do this was this steadily deteriorating situation as the COHA was breaking down, and in particular, my inability, because I wasn't being permitted to travel, to get -- or my convoys to travel, to get humanitarian supplies into those eastern enclaves that I discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next document, please. It's --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the binder. It's 65 ter number 9.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Add it's a document dated the 5th of April, 1995, and it purports to set forth what happened at the meeting on that day. Have you reviewed this document and is it an accurate account?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, please look at paragraph 49 of the statement. In this paragraph, you're talking about the week following your meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the 5th of May, so it's earlier -- I mean on the 5th of April. So it is early in April 1995, and you said: "The following week, the Bosnian Serb army closed Sarajevo airport to all but UNPROFOR military flights." I have a two-part question. What effect did that have on Sarajevo, and did it serve a military purpose?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: A military purpose for the Bosnian Serb, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It stopped the flow of humanitarian aid into the -- into Sarajevo, and its military purpose can only be supposed that, therefore, it weakened Sarajevo as a city under siege?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any weapons going through -- or weapons or military supplies going through the airport at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So was the sole effect of closing the airport to stop humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I can't say it was the absolute sole effect, but it certainly was a very, very large part of the effect. There would be over things that came might have in, personnel and so forth, that could no longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, have you a tendency to tell the witness what he is to say: Was the sole effect to stop humanitarian aid? Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was a follow-on from his previous answer, Your Honour, where he said that was the effect. I just wanted to know if there was any other effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But please try to elicit the evidence from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could look at paragraph 50, you describe an incident on the 21st of April when members of the contact group were effectively detained by the Bosnian Serbs at the airport and denied access. Did this serve any military purpose for the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 54, you describe how in early May the situation there Bosnia and around Sarajevo deteriorated, and you give specific examples of things that occurred on the 7th of May and the 7th and 8th of May. Then looking at paragraph 60, referring to a little bit later in May, you describe shelling occurring on a regular basis. And my question is this: At this time by April, May 1995, was there a change in the level of shelling and snipping that was occurring?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: During May, it increased in frequency. The number of attacks increased in frequency and in -- and also in the volume of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is that -- was that true both of shelling and sniping, or are you only referring to shelling?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Certainly the shelling, and I'm less confident that the sniping was increasing as much as the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that -- that increase continue or stop after May?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, we -- you have an incident which -- when -- because these weapons -- what's happening is not only has the COHA had broke down now, but previous things that preceded -- or arrangements that the preceded the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, which was the weapon collection points which were associated with the exclusion zones, had been something that had happened in the previous year, 1994. Those were breaking down as well, and what was happening is that the weapons in the collection points were beginning to be used and were being operated from the collection points in some cases. And this -- now, directly, this wasn't just a question of the UN forces standing between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnians, it was a question of now something that the UN was directly associated with; the exclusion zones and it's weapon collection points. This arrangement was starting to break down as well. And that had -- had grown up all through May. Towards the end of May - to look at the dates, I think I'm in paragraph 61 now, yes - it reaches a point where I had given an ultimatum. On the 25th of May, NATO is then called in to attack some targets, to try to re-establish the situation around these collection points and exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will talk about that in a moment. If we could come back it my question, which is: After May, in June, July, August, did the increased levels of shelling and sniping continue or did it change?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, I misunderstood. After May, and those incidents I've just started to describe, matters calmed down again in-- in June in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did they every flare up again?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. On and off, there were various incidents and so forth. But you get the -- if we go right into July and August, it -- you finish up with it flaring up again towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to assess whether control was being exercised, yes or no, by the Bosnian Serb army over this shelling and sniping of civilian areas; and if so, at what level was this control being exercised?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It was being -- yes, it was being controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you able to assess at what level it was being controlled, in your judgement, based on your observations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The control of the artillery fire is -- is conducted normally, and that is how I understood it around Sarajevo, at the level of the commander of the whole -- at the highest practical point. Therefore, I expected it to be controlled at Sarajevo corps level of the artillery fire. The sniping is not controlled in that way. That would be much lower down the hierarchy of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the reason for that distinction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's simply the range of the weapons is the driver. You can fire an artillery weapon on an 360-degree arc all the way out to its range. So -- let's suppose the range is 15 kilometres, then the -- this weapon -- I think my microphone is gone, perhaps not. This weapon can reach out to a circle of radius 15 kilometres. It tends to be commanded at that sort of level, because this weapon can be brought to bear to influence events across the whole of that area. A sniper is using a rifle range 4 to 600 metres in practical terms, and this would be controlled at a much lower level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apply the same kind of analysis to the shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shell is, as I said, an artillery weapon. I would have to go and check the weapons in that range. But in round terms, a radius of 15 kilometres the sort of radius that they can affect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so that would be commanded at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, I would except to see it controlled at the corps level, because that was the level of demand was associated with the siege of Sarajevo. Let me try and explain. When I say this, I'm -- if you have got that weapon there, you -- you've allocated it to a target. You've given the commander of that artillery a mission, a task, an order, which -- however you're doing that command. And if you go back to my mission arrangement, you, as a corps commander holding all your artillery together, because that covered the whole radius of your interest, you may still -- you would give an order perhaps, "You are to destroy anything crossing that river," or you might give him a mission, "You are to block any enemy movement across that river." And let him get on with and work out how he is going to do that, but you would still be directing that fire. Because you could then take it away and give it to support some other activity because that weapon could reach all the way across your geographic span of command. Does that help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in terms of hierarchy in the army, indeed, we have platoons, we have company, battalions, divisions and such. You said that in terms of sniping, it's at the lowest rank or level was for weaponry artillery that is at the higher level because the range is greater. In your experience in Sarajevo, at which level could decisions be made when it came to sniping operations? Was it at the level of a platoon or of a company? You know, I was talking about the autonomy earlier on. At which level could the decisions be made as to shelling of civilian locations? Was it also at the levels -- at a level of battalions or platoons or divisions? What is your explanation for all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer the question, or try to, first of all, theatrically and then try to apply it to the circumstances. The same logic that says that your artillery weapons are held at the highest level in terms of command, because that covers the range of this man's responsibilities, so you can follow that down to the sniper. Now, as a general rule, sniper operations are controlled at around battalion level. It's a specialist skill, and you -- and the weapon is -- it broadly of that range -- fits that range, scale, to the hierarchy. But I'm -- I was trying to explain about the -- how would you use the weapon. In -- it doesn't mean to say that you can't control the use of it at a higher level, even if the day-to-day or minute-by-minute activity is held at a lower level. For example, you can stop, you can give an order, "There is to be no use of snipers or only these types of targets are to be engaged." It is then left to the subordinate to act within those restraints on -- in executing any of his other missions that he is -- or orders that he has been given within that -- those restraining instructions of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many levels are there between the battalion and the sniper?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, again, each army is slightly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, tell us in terms of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, you had companies which is roughly 100 men; a battalion might be anywhere around 3 or 400 at best. In the Bosnian Serb, brigades were very small and varied in size according to the communities from which they were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, just to follow on your -- one of your previous answers, you said, "It doesn't mean that you can't control the use of it at a higher level," talking about sniping. Just so we're clear, could the corps command, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, speaking specifically about Sarajevo, could the corps level command have stopped the sniping or have directed it at practical targets?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, that could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described earlier there was sniping of civilian objects. Was that something that was well known?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That civilians were killed? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 56 of your statement, you describe an occasion when you were away and General Gobillard took over your duties while you were away. First question: Did that happen on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it did. This is the first occasion that he -- he acted add my deputy. The other occasion was in July when I was on leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you returned and resumed your duties, did you take over all of the -- did you take over the matters which he had been supervising?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Paragraph 61, you say that fighting flared up again in Sarajevo on the 24th of May, there was an ultimatum. On the 25th of May NATO bombed the Pale ammunition depot; and then, you say: "The BSA responded that evening by shelling all safe areas. One of the shells killed 71 people in Tuzla. My question is: When you say "shelling all safe area," does that include Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Certainly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at the next document, which is 65 ter 2376, I believe. Yes. It's a document dated the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I refrained from intervening so far, but it's been numerous times instead of the witness discussing what is contained in paragraph 1, instead he is being asked a direct question whether this shelling was at it was described there. Rather, the Prosecutor should have asked him what happened in Tuzla on that particular date. However, the question was leading, and it goes on and on and on. I'm not going to raise this issue again, but this will-- I just wanted to draw your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it was a leading question. I just asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the question? Let's find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question was: When you referred to safe areas, did that include Sarajevo? Because in the sentence, he says, "There is was shelling of all safe areas," and there were a number of safe areas. So the question was did that include Sarajevo. It's not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No that is not leading. But if you asked a question in the way that Mr. Tapuskovic put it, that would be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So there might be a tendency to do that, to simply have the witness affirm what was in the statement. If you were to say to the witness, what you said in paragraph 61 is accurate or is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I have already done that and it's in evidence. I'm not going to do that. I am just going to ask him if there are points to be clarified in his statement that's all I am doing: What does this mean? How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I indicated before, the evidence must come from the witness and not from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Could we look --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you seen 65 ter 2376?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that an accurate account of the events, including air-strikes, that were occurring at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could that be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P340, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 61, from page 13 -- which goes from page 13 to page 14, you talk about the Serbs taking some 400 UNPROFOR personnel hostage and using some as human shields cutting off utilities; then in the last sentence of the next paragraph, paragraph 62, you say that you determined that this action of taking hostages was determined and coordinated at the highest level in the Bosnian Serb army. My question is: What factors led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The fact that I had been rung up from -- by the Canadian-speaking liaison officer at Pale, that the first hostages taken were up at -- in the vicinity of Pale. The -- the spread of hostage taking across the whole of the -- it covered more than just the Sarajevo area and Pale area. It stretched out into the other parts of Serb-held Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next document. It's 65 ter 2382, and it's a document from the accused, dated the 27th of May, 1995. Drawing your attention to particular to point 1A and B, is this consistent with the events that are occurring at the time that you talk about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Incidentally, I might say it also shows an artillery regiment, albeit an anti-aircraft defence directly under the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see what is at point 1A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's further to the discussion about command. I just noticed that to all SRK units and by courier to anti-aircraft defence light artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's an example of what I mean, Mr. Whiting, by the evidence being as self-contained as possible, even though this it is 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I was referring to, of course, was the number of members of the UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations taken prisoner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I see. Well, that is a good point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that that be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is at 1A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I think the General said that is consistent with what he is talking about in his statement. If I could draw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In future, let us that evidence on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to point 3, where it says that Russian UNPROFOR members must not be taken prisoner and captured Russians must be freed. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It was obvious, at the time, that this was happening, since everyone else -- nationalities were being taken prisoner and not the Russians. This wasn't a great surprise, if one remembered that the Russians had got there at the time of the exclusion zones and had been introduced, as it were, into Sarajevo, first, and then became part of the UN force, and that they were -- their barracks were located or their camp was located on Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line. And, more recently, there had been plenty evidence that preceding my meeting that we have already discussed, I think it's the 5th of March at Jahorina, there was plenty of evidence that, before me, the Russians had been up at Jahorina as part of a previous meeting. We had seen the vehicles and some them had come in from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's a reference to that in paragraph 28 of your statement, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you ask the witness to explain what is the implication of what he just described. I understand from the General's testimony that just prior to meeting Mladic, at this location, they saw the Russian vehicles leaving the place, meaning that the Russians had then just met separately with the Serbs. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding of that event was that a Russian delegation at some level - I never found out how senior this was - had come from Belgrade. They had been met and escorted by elements of the Russian unit that were in UNPROFOR, and it this was the movement that had been reported to me in the first incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I imagine that you would have to have been informed of this prior to the operations carried by the Russian UNPROFOR soldiers, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically, in international command, you might suppose that everybody tells everybody what they're doing; practically, this does not occur at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have the -- the suspicion now that many things were going on under your nose without you knowing, to put it bluntly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that needs to be a suspicion. I'm sure it is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what are the implications for the Serb line of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have known what was going on in their area. But remember, two of the parties at least, the Bosnians and the Bosnian Serbs, to all intents and purposes, are at war with each other. They are doing everything they can possibly do to conceal their intentions and purpose from each other. You, in those circumstances, one or other party believes that they know about themselves. You introduce an UN force in there, neither party is going to declare its all to the third party, nor -- nor does the third party necessarily know what their own -- your own political parties are doing behind you in their own national form as opposed to in their international form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Just wait for the translation. But did the Russian UNPROFOR units report back to you what they had learned from their contacts, their independent contacts with the Serbian leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I say "no," on this occasion. There were occasions when the battalion commander told me what he learnt; but on this occasion, they were silent even when asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, you've indicated that there were certainly things occurring that you did not have knowledge of. You've also given evidence here about your understanding of certain things, like the nature of the command of the Bosnian Serb army, the strategy of the Bosnian Serb army with respect to Sarajevo. Does -- just so we're clear on this point, does the fact that there were certain things that you were not aware of cause you to doubt in any way your conclusions that you have given to us, your -- about those matters, about the command -- the nature of the command, about the strategy?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. As one has learnt more after the event, I have been reinforced in the views that I was holding at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could we look at paragraph 63, please. After the hostages are taken, the UN hostages, you have some telephone conversations with General Mladic and you describe them here. And in the second sentence of paragraph 63, which is on page 14, you say, in the first of these conversations, "I complimented Mladic for the attacks on the safe areas causing civilian casualties and for the attacks" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are already hearing this paragraph being read out, with respect to which the witness is expected to comment; therefore, we are hearing things being read out which presumably the witness should be talking about. He should just be reminded of certain things, and then let him take up and talk, instead of having Mr. Whiting reading out the whole content to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must remember, Mr. Tapuskovic, that this is 92 ter, and 92 ter allows the statement of a witness to be put in evidence in lieu of the witness giving evidence, so that in principle, we could just have, under 92 ter, the witness's statement. The witness need not be present here at all, but we have modified the procedure to a certain extent. And under 92 ter quite, quite frequently, the Prosecution adduces evidence from the witness on particular points. So I don't see anything improper about the Prosecutor reading the parts of the statement of the witness. Indeed, the witness has already, at the initial stage of the examination-in-chief, confirmed the accuracy of everything that is in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, there are times when the Prosecutor does tend to -- to lead, and I will be on the lookout for that, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm also on the lookout for it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the second sentence, you condemn Mladic, and then it says, "Mladic said he was sorry for the actions," and then blamed you and accused you of being crazy and unreasonable. My question is: When he said he was sorry for the actions, how did you understand those words? What did you mean those words to mean at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Just so much rhetoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- was he acknowledging that he had participated in those actions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Oh, without a doubt. There was never any question that as far as he and I were concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, that was leading that. That was leading. That was improper. You should ask him what did you mean. And, indeed, you did ask him and you didn't get the answer, so that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think in fairness, Your Honour, I think he misunderstood my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it would have to stop there. But it is not proper for to you put the answer in the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In paragraph 69, you talk about another conversation with General Mladic on the 28th of May. Could you look at the next document, which is 65 ter 42, and in particular the second page. Have you reviewed this document, and is it an accurate account of your phone conversation with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What the highlights of this conversation, General? Just give us a summary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, you have a large number of hostages taken of UN personnel, and there are - I think it's 2. I'd have to double-check - Serb soldiers taken by the French in an incident over a bridge in Sarajevo. And I am making the point, amongst others, that it is against the Geneva Protocols; it is also against -- to be wearing uniforms of the UN, to take hostages of UN forces and so forth; and that he is in breach of all of these positions, legal positions. I am asking for the release of all my soldiers, and equally telling that the two soldiers, under French control at the time, that they're being properly treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And his response, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The response is that we were getting nowhere at that stage. We're really stating our two negotiating positions, if you like. As I recall it at the time, he wasn't going to hand over the hostages without -- we weren't going to have a prisoner exchange, if you like, at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until this moment, I didn't know that the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, has not received the binder and that he cannot follow on the screen. He cannot see the documents being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And why is that? Mr. Whiting, did you transmit a copy of the binder to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we transmitted a copy of the binder to the Defence. The Defence has a binder and these -- I sort of thought that these would be called up on e-court as we were going along. But of course we have been were going so quickly, I accept that that probably has not occurred. I'm happy to let the accused have Sean's binder. I apologise for the oversight. Of course, I thought giving the Defence a copy -- I didn't think of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing. Only two of the documents are in B/C/S; the rest is in English, the documents in the binder; therefore, this is not an adequate for the accused to be able to inspect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that is not accurate. All the translations are included in the binder, as Your Honours can no doubt see. I think they are separated by green paper. With respect to each document, they appear in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, if you could look at paragraph 71, you talk about the Bosnian army -- you say, "The Bosnian army mounted a long heralded attack to break the siege of Sarajevo." How long did that attack last, to your memory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: My memory is some two to three days in the actual attack. There were some period afterwards as they withdrew and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could now look at the next document, which is 65 ter 43. It's a letter dated 26th of June, 1995. Is this your signature on the letter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why, if can you recall, was this letter written?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I think this was a case of me drawing together, if you like, towards the end of what had been a difficult month in the aftermath of the bombing an incidents in May the -- into one letter, my concerns as to the use of force, and incidents involving the people in the safe areas and so forth. I also note that in a week's time, I'm intending to go on leave, and I suspect for that reason I'm pulling everything together to make sure that I've made thing as easy as possible for my deputy when I'm away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the next document, please, and in particular skip the first two pages, I'm interested in page 3.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: And the next document is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 65 ter 824?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I just want to be sure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you can go to page 3, it's a document dated 22nd of August, 1995, purports to give an account of the meeting that you had with General Mladic. And focussing in particular on point 6, which is page 2 of this particular memorandum, could you tell us if this is an accurate account of the meeting and what the -- what the important points were in that meeting, briefly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. As is implied in the opening sentence of that -- of that paragraph, one is still trying to establish just who is speaking for the Bosnian Serbs. And the reason for this is that during the period of June, July, and that bit of August, if you like, the senior level arrangements in Pale had been coming under considerable pressure, particularly politically. And it wasn't entirely clear just what the relationship was between Karadzic and Mladic. If you remember earlier in evidence, I said that -- that there's never an absolutely precise line between the military and the political at the level we're talking, and here am I trying to establish just where that line was in this new set of circumstances. The other point that comes out from this is that by this stage, both Karadzic and Mladic had been indicted as war criminals after the incidents in -- of the collapse of the Srebrenica pocket, or enclave. And here he is saying, "I'm a war criminal, but have you to talk to me, have you to deal with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, General, I would like to ask you some questions about what is referred to as the Markale 2 incident in August. It's in paragraph 108 of your statement and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what information came to you at that time about what had occurred at Markale 2.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, Markale 2, just to situate the answer, refers to an attack from mortars, some fire rounds were fired, one of which killed 30 or so people in the marketplace at Markale. It's called 2 because there had been a previous incident the previous year of the same scale. The -- there was a procedure by which a group of people called the UNMOs, UN Military Observers, who were reporting organisation that was superimposed across the whole of the UN command in the Balkans and reported direct to Zagreb. They had the -- they would go and record all these incidents as one type of incident, so one source of reporting within the UN as a whole. It was also the responsibility of the sector commander, in this case Sector Sarajevo, to report, and he was part of my command. The UNMOs had a liaison officer, so I knew what they were doing. It wasn't that they were just free spirits, but they were separately commanded. So there were two sets of investigations took place with a slightly different sets of competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there any other investigations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Because of these two, we found ourselves with -- a certain amount of disagreement as to the -- what had occurred; and as a result, I directed a member of my staff to draw all of the reports together so that I could come to a single conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: -- or rather, come to a conclusion on a single set of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any of the investigations into this matter come to the conclusion that the shell that killed the 30 or more people had come from ABiH positions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 108 that: "After an investigation, I decided beyond a reasonable doubt that the rounds came from the Serb's side." What factors led you to come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Briefly, the direction -- there was a argument about the direction or two different views as to the direction these rounds came from, but that all took us outside the -- outside of Bosnian-held Sarajevo. The -- there with a was a radar called Cymbelline, which by deduction from the fact that there was no evidence from the radar that these mortars had been fired is that trajectory, therefore, was below the beam of the radar and this led you to the deduction that it was a fairly long range engagement. There was an acoustic system that didn't pick up any firing, which tells that it was out of range of the acoustic system, and we also had a number of observation posts; none of which reported hearing the firing as opposed to the explosion, all of which led me to the view that these rounds had been fired from outside the enclave, in the direction of one or other of these directions that had-- that the different views as to where they came from. And, finally, it is my experience of being in a siege that rounds that fall on the inside of the siege tend to come from outside the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, why was it important or necessary for you to reach a conclusion on this matter? Why were you trying to reach a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, it was my business, as the UN commander, to do this, not least because of the decisions made in the -- at the London Conference in, I think, it's the 21st and 22nd of July; anyway, towards the end of July of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 110, you recount a conversation that you have with General Mladic, and he proposes setting up a joint investigation team. What was your reaction to that proposal?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: This was not a new suggestion. It was new because this incident was new. But these types of joint investigation commissions had been proposed before on other incidents; and when they had been used, they had just become a method by which you got, yes, he did it, no, he didn't type of arguments and no decision was reached at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you also recount that Mladic stated that his staff had confirmed that no fire orders had been issued to his units. What was your reaction to that kind of information from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't believe it. I had no reason to suppose -- put it another way: He would say that, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, and I think you have already touched on this, but I will put the question nonetheless, do you have any reaction to the claim, the more general claim, that the ABiH was sniping and shelling its own people within the siege area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard those claims. I heard them when I was there. At no stage had I ever been shown any evidence to support such an assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Smith, I am counsel for the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, Commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I had an opportunity to examine you on some matters before and now I have been given another chance to ask questions concerning your stay in Sarajevo and your command duties. As I can see from your statement, and I have to start with that, according to paragraph 3 therein, you took over command of the United Nations Protection Force in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 23rd of January, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your predecessor was General Rupert Smith. Is that correct? Rose, General Rose.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a handing over the duties between the two of you once you arrived there? Did you meet with Rose before his departure from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I had visited Sarajevo in November of the previous year and had been briefed by General Rose, and we met in Zagreb rather than Sarajevo the day before I arrived Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet in Sarajevo the day of your arrival? I suppose General Rose was still there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. No. We met in Zagreb as I came through Zagreb to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that in November when you met him, and then subsequently in Zagreb, did you discuss with General Rose the situation in Sarajevo and were you trying to gain some information concerning the problems UNPROFOR was encountering in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn from him that after the event of the 5th of February, 1994, that is, after the first incident and the killing of people at Markale, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, during several months, violated cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't remember us going into that degree of detail, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he talk to you at all about who committed more violations of the cease-fire, which side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Which cease-fire are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
