utterances.text: Did General Rose tell you anything about the situation while he was UNPROFOR commander and did he tell you that in that period, especially after the Markale incident, for almost two months there was constant violating of the cease-fire by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't think we discussed those matters in that detail, which were almost a year old by the time we were having this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you something about his experience concerning the sniping activity in Sarajevo? And I'm particularly interested in one thing, and that is the thrust of my question: Did he complain to you about the fact that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the Muslim forces in Sarajevo, frequently opened fire on their own citizens trying to portray that as the activities of the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I don't remember him saying anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that General Rose, in his book called "Mission to Bosnia," when it comes to Markale 1, he wrote the following: "The initial investigation on the location made by the French experts showed that the approximate distance of a high building nearby the market made it impossible for any shell to land at the marketplace from a particular angle, which made them conclude that it was a mortar shell or that the actual detonation was carried out on the ground." Did he tell you anything about that, and were you able to read that in his book, since it was written in English?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Indeed, I have not read his book, and he didn't tell me that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, General Rose --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does counsel have, perhaps, a page reference for that citation? We'd be interested in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, give us the references.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference is in B/C/S, page 60. I wish I brought that book, because I also have it in English, but I didn't want to bring it in order to save time. Should the Court need it, I'm ready to forward it. I merely wanted to put to the witness what is said at page 60 of the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read out another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you this: "When a CNN reporter asked me why it was impossible to determine who fired that round, I told him that it is impossible to conclude based on only one round fired." Did you know that that figured as something that was discussed at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Tapuskovic, if you're going to place such reliance on that book, you really should have brought the English translation. But let's move on and see to what extent we need it. Not the English translation, the original English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received it from the OTP. I could have brought it along, but I simply wanted to ask the witness if things were, indeed, as they were described in the book. I didn't think it would be needed here for me to show it to you and to prove that I'm quoting correctly. Yet again, this may have been my mistake, but I was trying to save time. If the witness has no knowledge of it, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, quite often it's important to look at other passages in the book to see whether you have put the questions in a proper context. I don't say that you haven't, but that's one purpose that having the English original could serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After everything said, my question really is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Smith, did you know that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their government occasionally used their own people as victims in order to attain certain military and political goals. Were you aware of that, and were you warned of that by anyone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't know of it, no. I have heard the assertions, but nobody has ever shown me any evidence to support them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the assertions that you have heard, would you consider that the sources from which they came were credible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They always came from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from this transcript, your deputy was General Nicolai, and he testified before this Bench. At page 974 and 975, lines 17 through to 25 and lines 1 through to 10, at 975, he said, when asked whether it is correct that the Bosnians opened fire at their own people, Nicolai confirmed that from Van Baal, his predecessor, he heard that it is possible that things like that took place. Then he continues to say that there was a presumption of their intention to open fire at their own troops in order to try and show that as an activity of the other side. Did your deputy, Nicolai, convey to you what he had found out from Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: First of all, he wasn't my deputy; he was my Chief of Staff. He was of the headquarters. He wasn't my deputy commander. Again, I mean, I'm not sure I can comment on what someone else has said, except that in the way that you've described what had he said, it's still assertions. There is no evidence there and nobody every produced any evidence of this happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At page 975 and 976, lines 20 to 25, and line 1 to 16 of this case transcript, Nicolai said, and I'm reading from the transcript -- it is the transcript of this case when Nicolai said the following --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: If you're referring to Nicolai's transcript? Right, which I don't have so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of this case, this trial, and I'm quoting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have the references. Nicolai continues: "General Van Baal discussed a specific case where the Bosnian forces opened fire at their open people in order for the other side to be blamed for that. General Van Baal was fairly sure that that indeed took place." Did Nicolai, your Chief of Staff, draw your attention to that so as to bear that in mind when assessing what actions needed to be taken on your part?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't recall him doing anything of the sort. And who is General Van Baal? Where does he -- I don't recall a General Van Baal. He may have been there. I can't remember if he was or what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Van Baal was Nicolai's predecessor and that is what Nicolai learned from him.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: General Brinquemont was Nicolai's predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but when we come to Markale I'm going to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember, what was the evidence from Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The evidence is -- I think it's worth reading. It says: "General Van Baal, who was actually my predecessor's predecessor, told me before my departure ..." and I think it's fair -- it should be said that it was his strong impression "but they never had 100 per cent evidence of this." I'm reading directly from the transcript at page 975.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that help to clarify it, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who this man was. But we're talking about events before I'm there and of a -- if Nicolai says that that's what that man told him, then that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 964, line 12, General Nicolai says as follows: "Concerning provocations relating what was being done from Sarajevo by the BH army, a provocation may be fire from small-calibre weapons on Serbian positions. Another form of provocation could be fire from heavy weaponry. It is well known, inter alia, that vehicles with mortars mounted on them were used in order to shoot randomly at different positions of the Bosnian Serbs outside the city." Do you know anything about this, and did General Nicolai mention that to you and warn you about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, objection. That misquotes what General Nicolai said. He did not say "fire randomly"; he said "fire from arbitrary -- well, not arbitrary, but at various sites outside the city at Bosnian Serb territory." It doesn't say, at least in that passage, that they were firing randomly, as has been quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. With that qualification--

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the essence. Absolutely that's the essence. If we do need some interpretation or checking by the interpreters, but that was the essence of the matter. And if you remember, that is what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the word "randomly" in B/C/S, in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we're trying to find it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We devoted a long time, Your Honours, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us the line of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 12, page 964.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, he doesn't say it there but he does say it elsewhere, at page 997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Say what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He talks about random shooting at Serb territory; that is, General Nicolai does in this transcript. I have found it at 997, 998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of 997. "Is it not true ..." and then the answer, going on to 998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see it. This is a question from Mr. Tapuskovic. "Is it not true that the BH army soldiers were firing these shells randomly only in order to elicit a reaction from the army of Republika Srpska. Is that true, sir?" Answer: "Yes. That's the gist of the statement I made at the time." Well, on that basis the question can be put.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Nicolai came after you and was your Chief of Staff. You claim that General Nicolai would not have conveyed such a thing to you, which could be very important for subsequent actions, and you still claim that you didn't hear any of this from Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I do not remember him saying what has just been said that he said in court to me like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. But if we go to page 986, May 1995, and this is what Mr. Nicolai says about the NATO bombing, lines 17 to 22: "In mid-May there was a series of conflicts. Some of them were caused by the Bosnian Serbs and some of them were caused by the BH army. In one specific case involving the Jewish cemetery, the initiative came from the BH army. When we discussed this, that for this reason we are not going to attack the Serbs but, rather, address this issue with the BH army." My question is: At that time you advocated an immediate bombing of the Serbian positions, and after you had established that the provocation actually came from the BH army, you did not take this course.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Is that what General Nicolai is saying or are you asserting that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not asserting anything. I'm quoting the words of General Nicolai uttered before this Chamber. This is what he observed and said, and I'm asking you: You were in favour of bombing the VRS positions, but you gave up on the idea because that had been caused by a provocation on the part of BH army.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: If we're referring to the incident in which a number of people are killed at the entrance, at the Butmir entrance, to the tunnel under the airport, is that the incident we're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That's an entirely different part of the city, the Jewish cemetery, whereas the tunnel was in the Dobrinja area.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Indeed. I do not remember the particular case that you are referring to. But if my Chief of Staff, General Nicolai, recalls it like that, then I dare say -- and that is his memory of the decision I took and he said that, then it is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the question is: During your stay in Sarajevo, did you at any time have occasion to advocate an immediate bombing of Serbian positions after you had established that provocation actually came from the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was, I believe -- again, my memory, I'm trying to find the place in my own statement. But there was a case in early May -- yes, I have it here, paragraph 54. At that stage and at the opening stages of that, you can -- there is -- there's the attack that kills a number of people at the Butmir entrance and I decide against calling for an air-strike there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where in paragraph 54?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 54 in my own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where in that is there a reference to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In early May," and then "The 7th of May, a Serb shell or mortar round killed 11 people at the Butmir entrance," the second ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the kind of incident that counsel is referring to, nor, indeed, is it the kind of incident that I put in my question, which was whether at any time you had occasion to advocate -- well, I see now it might very well be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that here was a case where I decided not to call for an air-strike because I considered this was part of the fighting between the two sides and there were people in uniform involved. But during the evening, the situation changes and we now get repeated shelling of civilian areas and so I then change my decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, can we put it more simply, although, you have virtually said so when you say there was fighting between the two sides. But I wanted to ask you specifically whether you are able to isolate cases where provocation came initially from the BH army, and to which the Serbs responded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The very use of the word "provocation" is part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us -- sorry, let us delete the word "provocation." Let us say -- let us ask the question in a different way, whether you can isolate in your memory instances where fire came first initially from the BH army drawing a response from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can -- I'm confident that those incidents existed. If I got all the logs, I could probably find them for you. There was a war going on. We were standing around in the middle of it. And it's only as -- it's why I raised the point about the word "provocation." It was used by both parties to justify actions. It wasn't a reason for the action in the first place necessarily; justified subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I'm going to ask you about the tunnel. However, the Jewish cemetery is another part of the city and this situation prompted an immediate consideration of striking the positions of the Bosnian Serbs and not the positions of the BH army, although they were the ones who caused the incident. And here you insisted that an action be taken immediately against the Serbian side. However, you decided not to do that after you had learned that the Bosnian side were the ones who caused it and who probably deserved some punishment for that. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I wasn't there to punish anybody, first of all; and, secondly, I do not remember the incident in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the tunnel, paragraph 54, and I would like to remind you again -- in the transcript 982, lines 2 to 5, again, it's Mr. Nicolai's statement, and it's contained in the transcript of this trial, lines 2 to 5, page 982. And this is what he says about the tunnel as a military target. "Nicolai confirms that irrespective of where the entrance point or the exit point of the tunnel were, if troops were moving inside it, it could become a military target." Do you agree that if troops were entering or exiting the tunnel, the tunnel in that situation can become a military target?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It is the troops that are the military target, not the tunnel. The fact that they're there in the entrance makes that locality, where the troops are, a target. It's because the troops are there. They're the target, not the hole in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my question. Maybe I didn't formulate it precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the significance of the distinction that you make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the hole in the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the troops.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military target is the -- the significance of the military target is the military force, rather than specifically its locality. The military force might be using the locality to advantage, such as a hill with a church on it or whatever, and so that can then become a military target. But it's because the military are there, not because it exists as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly why I read out to you Nicolai's statement, that the troops moving and entering or exiting the tunnel were the target, and you just confirmed that. Can you please say without nodding your head.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, I do confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about paragraph 54. It says: "The Serb shell killed 11 people at the Butmir entrance to the tunnel, some of whom were in uniform." How do you know that all of them were not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't recall how that was -- that was deduced. Perhaps we had people there or perhaps the Bosnians only reported so many being in uniform. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR did not have observers on this location. The only report you could have received about this was from representatives of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't know we couldn't -- we didn't have someone there at that time, I'm sure, is correct. But there is no reason why we couldn't have driven someone there after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, Mr. Smith, is it that you were very firm in your request for immediate air-strikes against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces, although, as you yourself said and as Mr. Nicolai said, it was a legitimate target for the one who had perpetrated the attack. Nevertheless, you requested an immediate bombing of the Serbian side. However, after an assessment was made, it was -- this request was withdrawn -- actually, your request was denied by the HQ in Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, that isn't correct, and that isn't what I said in my statement. I said -- I decided against an air-strike; and then during the night, the shelling of Sarajevo continued, some of it falling on civilian areas. And it's at that point that I request the air-strike, which is -- is denied, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, in the last sentence, it says that the UN PF headquarters Zagreb denied your request. Look at your last sentence in paragraph 54?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That is correct. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, read from the middle of the paragraph 54. It says, "During that day, pressure for air-strikes grew; but on balance, it was decided not to request a strike at that time. However, during the night, 7th to 8th May, the shelling of Sarajevo continued, some of it falling in civilian areas, and an air-strike was requested. This was denied by headquarters, UN PF in Zagreb." That is consistent with what the witness just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, at the time when the shelling took place and when some of the shells landed in Sarajevo, maybe we can ask the witness if can he confirm that it was fired from one side only or was there an exchange of fire, but he persisted in requesting the air-strikes, which were denied by the Zagreb UN PF headquarters after certain checks were made. So Zagreb headquarters denied his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us ask the witness then. Are you able to confirm whether the shelling was from one side only or whether there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether there was an exchange of fire. I can -- I'm quite sure that there was shelling of civilian areas of Sarajevo, and the -- and it was because of that that I requested the air-strike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Shelling by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By the Serbs. Do you have any idea why your request for the air-strike was denied by the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primarily, my understanding at the time, and events have not changed this, this was primarily political rather military and was to do with the resolve of the Security Council and the troop-contributing nations to run the risks, if you will, of pursuing this course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to refer to another portion of Mr. Nicolai's testimony, pages 996 and 997, lines 21 to 25 and lines 1 to 25, which read as follows: "UNPROFOR's presumption was that UN points were deliberately targeted in the hope of the Serbs responding and hitting the UN personnel." Do you know anything about such events when fire was deliberately opened in the vicinity of UN points, checkpoints, in order to provoke Serbs into action and thereby have certain UN facilities being targeted and shot, and then blame laid on the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: This was by the Bosnians would -- would fire close from an UN position thus causing Bosnian Serbs to shoot back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please to turn off the microphone because we cannot hear the witness if you are talking at the same time. My apologies. I was not able to interpret what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are being asked by the interpreter to switch off the microphone when the witness is speaking; otherwise, the interpreter has difficulty hearing. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to be clear that the question was that the Bosnian Muslims would fire from positions very close to a UN position, in the hopes of provoking a counterfire from the Bosnian Serbs that would hit the UN position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is what Nicolai also said. This is not based on isolated incidents. This was happening on a regular basis, that fire came from the vicinity of UN points by the BH army. In November 1996, he said that he saw Bosniaks firing from the vicinity of the UN building using mobile mortars of small calibre. Nicolai also confirmed what he said earlier, that very often these positions were very often close to UN positions, such as the PTT building, the UNHCR, the ice-rink, and the Marshal Tito barracks. Did you have this information and is this what Mr. Nicolai is saying is true?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I have the information and had it at the time that firing took place from positions in close proximity to UN positions and this drew return fire. The -- on the other hand, at no stage did I ever get any hard concrete evidence that this was a deliberate act to provoke an attack upon the UN. The suspicion that I think Nicolai is referring to is rather more that - and this occurred with both sides - we, the UN, were used as a shield for their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, please, what is discussed hear is that Mr. Nicolai saw fire being opened from mobile objects, such as trucks, when shells were fired; and then that particular object would immediately be moved and they simply want to the provoke a reaction on the part of the Serbs. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I know that some of these incidents took place. I do not know that the purpose was to provoke an attack on the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you disagree with the assertion of General Nicolai. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I'm not disagreeing that some of these incidents take place nor -- I think use the word the "supposition." We didn't suppose that this might be the case. But on no occasion did I have evidence, concrete evidence that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Nicolai stated this categorically. It was no supposition. It was his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object on two grounds. The first is that in the testimony that Nicolai says -- speaks about the assumption, but, secondly, I think this question has been asked now three or four times now and the General has answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I uphold the latter objection. Mr. Tapuskovic, you have ventilated this point sufficiently. The witness has answered. In my view, there is nothing more to extract from him. We have to make up our minds what we make of his evidence, as well as that of General Nicolai. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's another important thing with which I will conclude this topic. General Nicolai believed that one single round would not be enough to deal with such a source of fire, but, rather, that a number of rounds should be used to neutralise such an object, such a position, and such positions existed throughout the city. Therefore, I wanted to see Mr. Smith's reaction to that. How do you neutralise such a target?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that or would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it, but I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, reformulate the question so it's more intelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A mobile mortar fires a single shell and then moves away. Can it be neutralised by using a single round, or would one have to use a number of shells to do away with such a source of fire?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It is the normal practice to fire mortar rounds in particular and artillery rounds in a number of rounds at a time. The -- in the case of this particular fighting around Sarajevo, the Bosnian army had very few, if any, of the heavier weapons and the -- of the types of heavy weapons. They had some mortars, and they used them, as I observed it, as single barrels instead of in batteries or sections of weapons where you have more than one. This was because of a scarcity of the weapons and their ammunition rather than any desire to use them in that way, in the first instance. To some extent, this applies to the Bosnian Serbs as well, but they had more of these weapons and tended to use them in the more convention way and so would you get a return fire where you would get a Salvo fired rather than a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Smith, in paragraph 6, you talk about your relationship with Dr. Alija Izetbegovic, the late Bosnian President. In the last sentence, you say: "I think our relationship developed to one of mutual respect an understanding. He was always available to me." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to your -- to the period of your command. Did you know that the tunnel that was used for the movement of troops was also used to, as described in his book during the time you were there, to transport hundreds of thousands of tons of weaponry into Sarajevo? Did you know of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I couldn't vouch for the quantity, but I was aware that weapons, as well as troops, would move in that tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the material time discussed here, this being the final months of 1994 and the whole of 1995, that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was better equipped and had better weapons than the army of Republika Srpska, even according to the testimony of some of your officers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I didn't see it like that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Alija Izetbegovic use to tell you about the fact that 20 to 30 planes during the offensive in June arrived loaded with weapons for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that those planes originated from some Islamic countries?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the fact that on the 27th of August, 1995, exactly one day before Markale 2, Alija Izetbegovic went to Paris?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had no knowledge of the fact that the commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina left Sarajevo on the 28th. Your service had no knowledge of that; rather, it was on the 27th of August. You didn't know that he left Sarajevo. You were not notified of the commander leaving the positions of his army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. There was no reason for him to do so. There was no requirement for this information to be passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, before you move to another topic, I wanted the General to give us his assessment of the relative strength of the two armies in terms of their weaponry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understood it at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnia-Herzegovina army was numerically larger than the Bosnian Serb army. It was re-arming; it was getting new weapons. The Bosnian Serbs were largely equipped with the weapons of the former army and were able to draw, to an extent at least, and I could never work out precisely the extent, on the army in Serbia for assistance, particularly in terms of logistic supply and materiel support. The Bosnian Serb army was better organised had a more professional corps of officers, and the Bosnia-Herzegovina army was in this regard struggling to create, if I can call it this, the nervous system to be able to use their new army effectively. I think that was the broadly the balance that I struck between them. Is that sufficient for you, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But more specifically, in terms of weapons, do you have an assessment of which army was stronger and in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By -- at that stage, and particularly remember Sarajevo is under siege, the balance of heavy weapons, by which I take everything from an 81-millimetre mortar upwards, lay with the Bosnian Serbs. The balance of advantage lay to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the composition of the Command Cadre beginning with Colonel Delic, Prevljak and a number of other officers, weren't there at least as many people on the Bosnian side who originated from the former JNA. I dare say even more than there were on the Serbian side, in the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That may have been so, but what it didn't give them and why I used the word "nervous system," you require more than the individual to make the machinery work. There has to be a staff system, there has to be people trained to make the organisation work, and to have the headquarters structures, the communication systems, and so forth, to transmit orders and so forth. By and large, those all lay with the Bosnian Serbs and not the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly, when it comes to Sarajevo, did you know at all that the fighters of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were exclusively people who have been living for hundreds of years at the places close to their positions. These were ordinary men who were -- who turned soldiers because of the situation itself.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That doesn't surprise me. The whole basis of the army of the former Yugoslavia was one for territorial defence, and it was built up that way. So what you just said does not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time, in addition to the sanctions imposed by the international community on the army of Republika Srpska, there were also sanctions in place imposed by the FRY as regards the Bosnian Serbs. At the Drina, such sanctions were imposed in preventing, first and foremost, any movement of any weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't able to progress much, and I'm still with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also had contact with Haris Silajdzic, who was a representative of the Bosnian government, and this is in paragraph 8 of your statement. You say you had meetings with him, which were the most numerous on the eve of the initial NATO air-strikes in May. Did Haris Silajdzic continuously demand from you that steps be taken in order to do away from the embargo for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to begin with NATO bombardment of the Serb positions? Did he use any available opportunity to stress that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly after your meetings, indeed, we saw the first NATO air-strikes against Serb positions, or is that a mere coincidence? Is it related?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I wasn't meeting Silajdzic to discuss NATO bombing, no. Later in that paragraph, I tell you why I meet with Silajdzic because he is a part of an opposition, and it gives me a better understanding of what's going on inside Bosnian politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you mention General Mustafa Hajrulahovic, aka Talijan. There you say he was a senior staff officer with the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That's what I understood at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In a document that I have in my hands, rather in the document, and I received it from the archives of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army, there is a piece of information concerning an event of the 5th of August, 1995 -- 1994. Do you remember what took place on that day, and did you intervene concerning that incident? It concerns an air-strike of the 5th of August, 1994, and this is what the gentleman, who drafted this report, is telling us there. It is 1994. I know you weren't there, but you prevented or put a stop to an action, since you were the commander of NATO forces for southern Europe. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I don't know what you're talking about in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read it out for you. He says in that report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you reading and where from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if it could be shown to the witness and to us also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no translation. It is General Mustafa Hajrulahovic reporting on an event of the 5th of August. An air bombardment which was prevented because -- it is a 65 ter document, number 01958 received from the Prosecutor. And this was within the 65 ter batch, and the number is 01958?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have copies for us, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless, it is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just asking, do you have copies, as you should, for the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I do. But the reference was wrong, Leighton Smith; where as, this is Mr. Rupert Smith. Therefore, I will have to introduce this document when we have General Rose's testimony. This is another individual, Leighton Smith. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just stop you for a minute, though, to discuss an administrative matter. Mr. Whiting, the arrangement that was made yesterday was that Mr. Hadzic would conclude his testimony at 1.00 p.m., from 1.00 to 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be wrong, it happens, but my understanding was that the witness would be available from 1.00 on, in the event that General Smith finished, but that he is available to finish his testimony tomorrow. So if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand that. I thought that because of his health you wanted to conclude with him today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can find out by e-mail. It will take about five minutes. I will find out and I will report to the Chamber what the arrangement is. I could be wrong. That was my understanding, but I could be wrong. I wasn't involved in making the arrangements. I will find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have time for one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have just gotten an e-mail. They're watching outside the courtroom. Apparently, what I said is correct, the witness could finish tomorrow. So if we could finish with General Smith today, we would be really grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apparently, he would be. Yes, let us continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to open up a new topic since it has to do with paragraphs 16 and 21. Paragraph 16 speaks about Radovan Karadzic and his meetings with General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we're going to start a new topic, we will take a break now and resume in 20 minutes. And when we resume, there are a couple of administrative matters that I would like to raise before the witness is brought in, just for five minutes. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you were to give me a report today on the efforts being made to get Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have heard from him. He can come on the date that we propose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. And what I was planning on doing this afternoon after court was putting this in a memo to Your Honours with the details, but the answer is, yes, he can come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And is there any news about the unknown UNMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I don't expect there to be news. That would take a matter of weeks rather than days to get that person identified. We have a name for that person; but to get any further information, I expect is going to take more like weeks than days. We are going to -- as I indicated, our information is that it's a Kenyan individual, and it is my plan, in fact I may even try to do it today, to arrange a meeting with Kenyan embassy to see if we can do anything to expedite the matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They should be able to identify him if was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour. If I had a penny for every "should," then I would be a rich man. It shouldn't be a problem, but our experience in the past is that sometimes this can be very difficult. So I will do everything I can, and as I indicated in my memo, if we are unsuccessful in our efforts, we will certainly call on the Trial Chamber's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be brought in as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, paragraphs 16 and 21, you describe your meetings and relationships with Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic. First of all, let me deal with a documents tendered by the Prosecution as their exhibits, P336. We'll start with that one. And if we can -- if you could please at least look for a moment at page 1 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think have you to give him the 65 ter number, because that's how the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us the some more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 00089, entered as Prosecution Exhibit P336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But which one is that, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the second document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Witness, it's the second document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you looked at this document. It's been signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, commander-in-chief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Let me get to the back of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic held the highest position in the army of Republika Srpska. As President of the republic, he was the a commander in chief of the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the subheadings in this document on page 1, item 1, it reads as follows: "Main characteristics of the international military and political situation." Is that what is written here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find anywhere in this document any reference to any announcement or any order to shell Sarajevo or to expose it to sniping?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did, but let's just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, if that case it will take you at least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I can go to the bit that concerns this Sarajevo corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show it to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Page 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remember the pagination is different in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 9 in the B/C/S version, and it refers precisely to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In this passage, is there any reference to shelling and sniping on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you read this carefully, does it constitute certain general guidelines governing the operation of the VRS with a view to achieving specific military goals?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It's a directive. It says it is in the covering letter by General Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the beginning of the document, page 3 in the B/C/S version, and perhaps page 4 in the English version. It refers to the Muslim armed forces. Take a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, it is page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last sentences of the first paragraph, which mainly talks about launching counter-offensive actions, should NATO air force be used.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It is discussing the use of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this document is dated the 8th of March, 1995, which is only one month after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- it comes in on the 8th of March, a bit more than a month after my arrival, but, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now go back to the previous page, which refers to the Muslim armed forces. You said, in paragraph 3, it says, "The BH army is organised in six corps, 112 brigades, and 45 independent battalions, artillery battalions, numbering approximately 270.000 men. They have about 120 tanks, 80 APCs, 340 artillery pieces, 90 multi-barrel rocket launchers, 230 light missile launchers, 1800 mortars, 450 anti-aircraft guns, 700 anti-aircraft machine-guns, 200 anti-aircraft missiles stinger, 370 anti-armour rockets, 16 transport helicopters, and 17 sport and agriculture aircraft." During your stay and mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when flying over this position, are you able to note at least approximately the -- that there were as many men as stated here inside Sarajevo and outside it, as well as all the weapons listed here.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I saw no evidence to support that amount of weapons even in little bits. If that's correct, they were very well concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would that alter the answer that you gave to my question as to the relative balance of power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I don't know, in my memory, have no memory of that sort of concentration of weapons that I saw as I travelled around in the possession of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army as a whole. I'm not talking about inside Sarajevo. There was very little heavy weapons inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did say a while ago that it is possible that you did not have an insight into the whole situation, provided these weapons were well camouflaged, especially in the natural environment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I would draw a distinction between inside Sarajevo and more generally in Bosnian itself. In -- I am confident in saying that that sort -- those sorts of weapons were not available in anything like those numbers inside Sarajevo. If they existed outside Sarajevo, then I and my command were not seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something else. Wouldn't have been much more easier for this heavy weaponry to be camouflaged, particularly inside Sarajevo. Do you know anything about this, and do you allow for the possibility that they were also we will camouflaged inside the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It is always possible that some might have been, but they were not there in anything like those numbers. And I, from memory, I think there were about two or three tanks, and they were in a weapon-controlled point and were under my control. There was -- I don't think there was a single artillery piece or artillery -- or rocket launcher inside Sarajevo. If there was, it was one or two of artillery pieces, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the offensive in mid-June, which you say lasted only three days, most of the weapons listed here was being used on the front lines dividing the Serbian forces and the Muslim forces. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: My memory was they were not being used. Those weapons in those quantities were not being used on -- in that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you spent time in Sarajevo and probably flew over Sarajevo in a helicopter or in any other way, can you read anything from this map here behind you about the demarcation lines, since you're a military person.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I can recognise where I am. Sorry. Is that already for the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber the significance of the blue lines and of the red lines, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: To my understanding, the blue line is the Bosnian forward defensive line and the red the Bosnian Serb forward defensive line. The yellow marking, in the narrow a bit, is the airfield, and Sarajevo is, I think, it's marked IK on the inside of the small pocket that can you see enclosed in red. The high ground of Igman is in the south-west of the -- of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you spoke about this, it was -- you said that it was common knowledge that the tunnel was used for exiting Sarajevo. Did you know that the BH army used this tunnel to take up positions outside of Sarajevo, the positions marked with blue?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I knew the tunnel was used by their military. In which direction people were being moved, I don't know necessarily, unless one learnt it by some other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the June offensive engulfed all the demarcation line. Do you know that on all these positions, blue positions as well as inside Sarajevo itself and along all these markings, attacks were launched with several BH corps with a considerable amount of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I know that that attack occurred. The one that I could observe -- or those attacks occurred, and I apologize. The attack one that I observed, because I was there, was mounted out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand you. You were observing the conflict along these outer lines or in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I was inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, this document, P336, was something that was primarily the duty of the VRS commander, and that is General Mladic. He would be the first in line to comply with this, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: We're talking of this directive. Yes. This is his Chief of Staff passing it on to his corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this directive should have been implemented, first and foremost, by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Indeed. He is -- it's the same headquarters that's initiating the document as his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If that is the case, then the next document that I would like to show you is 65 ter 02267, admitted as P33. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that a decision passed by General Mladic based on the directive received from the commander-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please turn to next page. And, generally speaking throughout this document, can you tell me is there any reference at all to an order being issued to shell Sarajevo, to open sniping fire in the period after the 31st of March. Is there any mention of that at all?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. But I'm just trying to be sure, because I can't find -- he's writing specific instructions. Where is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at tasks of the army of Republika Srpska. I'm not going to read all of it. It just said to defend the territory of Republika Srpska. Is that what it says? That's is at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes. I was trying to find the specific instructions to the corps, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on page 6, if it's of assistance, 5.5.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Ah, there it goes. And all he is doing is telling the corps commander to carry out the task given in the directive number 7 that he has already received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, would it be fair to say that General Mladic issued ordered to all corps, including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; that is to say, to General Dragomir Milosevic, in the spirit of the decision?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the -- this is the order -- this is him doing this, in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, let us now move to paragraph 21 where you talk about your meetings with General Ratko Mladic. I'm not going to read the whole passage but, if necessary and if Chamber so desires, I would gladly oblige. So close to the beginning, you say as follows: "Mladic was -- Mladic is a soldier first and a politician second." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Well, it goes back to an earlier answer. When you are functioning at this very senior level, inevitably, what you are doing is political, and the point I was trying to make there was that he saw himself in the first instances as the soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "And that he never gave a thought to draw any political profit from his actions."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Are you asking me that as a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. He clearly did have political views. But when deciding how to act and so forth, he saw his primary responsibility to be that of military, not of the political.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You might say different if you deemed so, but you say here that he was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate which part of the passage he is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what part of the passage are you reading? Please indicate for the benefit of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 21, towards the end where it says -- where General Smith says, "He was brave and resolute and remained rational and in control under pressure. I believe he was driven by a single overreaching aim of the defence of the Bosnian Serbs and all else was to be subordinated to the achievement of this aim." This is what you said and this is what your assessment and view was, based on your meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 65 ter 00042, Prosecution Exhibit P342.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a telephone conversation between yourself and Mladic of 28th May, 1995. In paragraph 1, you said that he demanded that all flights of NATO transport aircraft be suspended. That was the practice that prevailed in the days before that. Is that what he demanded?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That he demanded the cessation of all NATO combat and transport flights. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But let me draw your attention to the very end of this conversation, i.e., paragraph 12 of your telephone conversation, and it read as follows. "General Smith said that he was not in command of NATO forces nor did he correct their actions. Mladic said he knew this to be a lie as into the could not act without his request. General Smith said that was absolutely correct. He was one of those responsible for recommending an attack, but he did not command NATO forces." Is it true that this is what you said in this telephone conversation, i.e., that you were not the person commending NATO forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was commanding then if you commanded UNPROFOR? When you made your decisions, who was in command, especially when we talk about the initial stages of air-strikes after Markale?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The command of the NATO force rested with NATO commanders. One of whom was Admiral Leighton Smith. He was at Naples. This chain of command all the way up to the North Atlantic Council in Brussels. I was in the UN chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Down it goes for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There goes my Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hope not. But, Mr. Tapuskovic, how is the command structure of NATO relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was about to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, in the evening, you ordered that NATO aircraft be put on ready for an attack on Serbian positions. That was the same day of the Markale 2 incident. That is what is in your statement. I can refer you to it, if you wish, and I was about to come to that. On the 28th, you decided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I still don't see the relevance. What if there was an order for NATO aircraft to be put on the ready for attack on Serbian positions on the same day as the Markale incident, is it a part of your case that NATO aircraft was responsible for the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Rather, that even before it was established what took place on Markale, because on the 28th there was still no knowledge of it - and we may go back to that report - and no final investigation was made as regards Markale 2, still there was an order to carry out that and to employ NATO aviation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what you're say is that NATO pre-determined the question of responsibility for Markale 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And that even before the conclusion of investigation, General Smith, who did not have any say in it, goes on with the bombardment which followed the day later, and I have proof of that, that I was about to put forth once I have reached the Markale stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm still not seeing the connection to the question of the liability of the accused, even if NATO did make that pre-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Dragomir Milosevic is not responsible for the massacre at the flea market on the 28th, and I intend to show that before this Bench. Still that incident was used for massive bombardments which lasted for days on the Serbian military positions, which resulted in many civilian victims. And it is our position that the whole activity that followed was not based on the -- on anything that was done by the Serb forces and that took place at Markale; rather, it was done by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. The connection appears to be tenuous, but continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being reminded by the members of my team that the part when I said that NATO sided with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that that part is missing from the transcript. That is why I wanted to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you talk about the fact that Croats were advancing in the southern part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the last sentence you say, in the last sentence of that paragraph you say: "The Bosnians had also used the air strip at Tuzla for light aircraft at night, which caused a degree of friction when NATO and the United Nations." Therefore, you allowed sorties of the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. The paragraph, and in particular the last sentence of paragraph 22 that you refer to, is that by our own observations and by complaints from General Mladic we were aware that some light aeroplanes were using this air strip. The control of the no-fly zone was the business of NATO, and they were saying this was not happening. We were not -- these flights were not occurring. And we were saying we could see them and that was the friction that was being caused. We were certainly not allowing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you want the to clarify that you had said that NATO was acting in collusion with the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that although my teammates are telling me that it wasn't reflected in the transcript. I intended to show that during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind. I am saying that your case becomes more understandable as to the relevance of the NATO attacks coming even before the issue of responsibility had been determined. I'm saying that I understand your case now. I mean, whether the evidence bears it out is another matter. But I said let's see the relevance if your case is that NATO was in collusion, was in collaboration with the BH army. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That, too, yes. But to go back to paragraph 24, you literally state the Bosnians had also used the air strip at Tuzla for light aircraft at night. You knew expressly that the Bosnians use the Tuzla air strip for night flights. Do you deny that now?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had another air strip at Visiko, and they flew from there as well for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I discovered that much later. In fact, I think in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh, you found it out, okay. I didn't hear that. But in the sentence before you said: "The Bosnian army was making open preparations to fight on in the spring." Therefore, at that time you were already familiar with their preparations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In no detail, but I knew they were preparing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 27, when talking about a meeting with General Mladic, you said that: "It became apparent that the Bosnian Serbs had decided that war was inevitable." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: They knew it was inevitable because the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina incessantly prepared for an offensive. They were getting ready to respond, should such a offensive take place. Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29, when Mladic complained to you of the sanctions imposed for the Bosnian Serbs, wasn't he actually asking that UNPROFOR be even-handed in the treatment of both sides so that the Serb side could also get some food and other supplies? Was that the thrust of his request, that UNPROFOR change it's strategy somewhat, so as not to only assist only the Bosnian side and to forward some of the humanitarian aid to the Serb side as well, as you continue mentioning in paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. In the first paragraph, he is -- wanting to see that the sanctions are lifted, and the sanctions were not about humanitarian aid. The sanctions were all about the supply of weapons and so forth. The second paragraph deals with humanitarian aid, and humanitarian aid is not part of a sanctions regime. And it is delivered to those in need, and those in need were in the enclaves. It is two quite separate issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Weren't the Serbs, particularly at the Sarajevo positions, in an enclave of sorts and a quite rigorous one too, as we can see on the map that just collapsed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: And there was a substantial aid programme supporting that -- or those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 38, you mention a plane that was hit by the Bosnian Serbs. I saw no proof, no pieces of evidence that it was done by the Serbs. It was done by Dobrinja, and Mojmilo was there overlooking the airport in the hands of the Muslim. What proof can you put forth that the Serbs did that, when that hill was in the hands of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: At this stage, I can give you no proof at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you do say that subsequent investigations proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the aircraft was engaged by a Bosnian Serb heavy machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, and I believe that was the case. But my ability to prove it now, I can't do that for you, nor I do think this was a matter of contention at the time. This was agreed by Mladic when it was complained about that this had been their people -- his people who had fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Excuse me. And what was the reason for the firing of this aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we ever properly understood that. I think it was one of the small aeroplanes that was used by Akashi, and I have a suspicion this was as much to frighten him as anything. But I can't -- that is purely another suspicion rather than anything I can prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a United Nations convention which is devoted to the protection of UN personnel, and this attack would have been in breach of that convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said what Judge Robinson said. You confirmed beyond any reasonable doubt where the fire originated from, but you said you have no proof of it. For the first time, however, you say now that Mladic admitted that. Who did he admit it to, when, and where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it's not the first time he has said so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said that during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the plane?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. That subsequently Mladic conceded that the attack was done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did he admit it to? You know that an admission is no evidence in and of itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the General explain again how that concession or agreement was made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this event, if it wasn't me, it was Akashi's staff, but we were all together at the time, complained of this event, protested about it. And my memory is that it was acknowledged by Mladic and the Bosnian Serbs that this had been their action, that it had been them that had fired on the aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mladic wouldn't talk to just anyone. Judging by the documents, I could see these were mostly reputable people and UNPROFOR officials, high officials. It could have been a conversation with a junior officer. Who did he admit that to? He could have talked to you or to Nicolai. Who did he acknowledge it to? Perhaps you can tell us something that can be taken into account by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I think it was immediately after this event this complaint went in and -- after all, it was Mr. Akashi and his officials who were in the aeroplane, as was I, when it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you that. I'm not disputing that. I'm asking you about a very important matter. General Mladic took great care of what he was saying and who he was talking to. Who did he concede it to, so as to enable us to take judicial notice of that, something that may help the Bench make their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to skip over a number of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I do take note of the time and I am just wondering if it's possible to finish with the witness today. I know I shortened my direct examination - I dropped half of the documents I was planning on using - to try to expedite matters. I think that, in my respectful opinion, that the cross-examination has spent a lot of time on areas outside the indictment. It seems to me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not for to you say, Mr. Whiting. We're in charge of the court, and if any question had been asked which is improper then we would have disallowed it. You must come on another basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they were improper. All I'm saying is there's been enough time to for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's for us to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. I can only make a suggestion, and that's all I'm trying to do. I'm just trying to raise the matter. Of course it's in Your Honours' determination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have that in mind. We may be able to continue for maybe 10 or 15 minutes, but there is a case in this courtroom this afternoon. Mr. Tapuskovic, how much longer will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I skipped at least 20 or 30 paragraphs now. I'm doing my best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you're not obliged to ask a question on every paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that. But virtually each and every paragraph is important. I'm now choosing the most important ones. I was told I was going to have three hours at my disposal for my cross-examination. Believe me, it is the minimum amount of time for me to go through all the issues that I must open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy, I understand, has the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will consult on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a difficult situation in terms of logistics. The counsel for the Defence has used just under two hours. He was allocated three hours. Bear in mind that I think five hours had initially been set aside for this witness. We could sit longer but the courtroom is not available. We could longer because Judge Mindua is not sitting this afternoon, and it seems therefore that in the interests of the proper administration of this case, Sir Rupert will either have to come tomorrow or come at another time if tomorrow is not convenient. May I inquire from you, General, whether you are available for tomorrow or would some other time be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to be in Brussels tonight to sign a document if nothing else. I am -- it would take me a couple of telephone calls to find out how easy it is to then get on a train and get back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can tell you because I take the train all the time. It leaves from Holland Spoor five minutes after the hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. It was freeing myself up at some other end and thus making some other arrangements. Does the Court sit on Fridays?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This Friday, no, we're not sitting. No, we're not sitting this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could be back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. We need a couple of telephone calls to establish. It's delivering this document and so on and so forth. It's a purely personal matter but have I to go and sign it, and getting it in the right hands to get back on the train and get back up here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
