utterances.text: We'll leave that to you to sort out and you will inform the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. We will resume either with you or with Mr. Hadzic, because we have to give counsel for the Defence reasonable time in which to conclude his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that. I do note that just looking at the calendar that courtroom I is free from -- after 3.30 this afternoon it appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We made an inquiry and were told no courtroom was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that courtroom I is available at 3.30 because the case finishes at that time, but will it finish? Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have in mind the mere physical ability to do all this. Now I have to wait for an hour and a half, although I have spent the whole day on my feet. I will do that if ordered, but I believe it would be much more convenient for General Smith to return another day. But, of course if I'm ordered to do so, I will wait for an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we can meet at 3.30, we will meet at 3.30. You are a young, strong man, Mr. Tapuskovic. You can't plead infirmity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm 70 years old, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 70 years young.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My guess is since the last case finishes at 3.30, my guess is that we would could only start at 4.00, because ordinarily they need a gap to load the tapes and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm worried knowing how the how the law courts run here. Will they finish at 3.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in that case, they have been sitting from 9.00 in the morning in that case. It's an all day and so I would except that they will be done by 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, if we were to sit from 4.00 to 6.00 this afternoon, would that enable you to get to Brussels in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would suit me best of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we will adjourn and resume in Courtroom I at 4.00. --- Break taken at 1.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, of course, you remain subject to the declaration that you made. Mr. Tapuskovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Smith, let me first ask you a few things about your meeting with Karadzic on the 5th of April, 1995. That's 65 ter 009, Prosecution Exhibit P339.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't have any of those documents. Thank you very much. 009. Yep, I have that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's your meeting with Karadzic on the 5th of April; and in item 2, there's mention of what -- of the items and issues that you dealt with, and I would like to hear something about item 3, which says: "General Smith pointed out his serious concerns with some recent actions attributed to the BSA; specifically, these were an increasing number of attacks on safe areas and breaches of the total exclusion zones." Do you remember discussing this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I remember the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And further on, you said that generally speaking these actions contributed to raising -- rising tensions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you added the following, that eventually you would be compelled to respond by NATO air-strikes and that this would not be in the interests of the Bosnian Serbs. Again, so you reiterated as early as on the 5th of April that the Serbian side would be subjected to NATO bombing, if they continued to behave as you described in your conversation with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, if they continued to attack safe areas and breach the exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, based on Karadzic's statement, that these exclusion zones were often abused, that the BH army left these zones and attacked civilian places, especially in the area of Srebrenica, and that was committed particularly by Oric. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The exclusion zones were the exclusion of the use of heavy weapons. They weren't in themselves exclusions to combat as such. And I was aware that the Bosnian forces were operating outside and from out from the safe areas, such as Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And if the Serbian forces would respond to that, was it really necessary to threaten them immediately with NATO strikes, if they didn't have any other option than at that protect the civilian population, and that is what Karadzic said, if I understand it correctly, what you discussed in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't remember, and I don't think it's said that that paragraph 3, the civilian population as such. My point was that the exclusion zones were being breached and the safe areas were being attacked, and that was something that NATO air-strikes was supposed to be called upon if that continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, NATO air-strikes were not an option when exclusion zones were abused and left in order to attack Serbian positions and most of all Serbian civilians. NATO was not necessary in these situations, was it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. The exclusion zone was that were no heavy weapons to be used within that zone, and the heavy weapons were collected in the weapon collection points. That was an exclusion zone. The attacks on civilians occur -- the point of the exclusion zone was to limit a type of weapon, rather than to specifically prescribe the attacks on civilians. That is prescribed by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, which talks specifically about safe area, reads: "General Smith explained that as an UN commander he had to ensure that mandates on safe areas were applied, and that those instructions connect him to the employment of NATO air power if safe areas are attacked." What was basically what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say: "Karadzic clearly views the SAs as BH strongholds. He made it quite clear he views the application on the SA mandate as illegal in international law." Is that what he said?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That is what we understood him to be something and my -- I don't have the back page, but I this is Colonel Baxter's report of my -- of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also say on that occasion that in his view the safe area and exclusion agreements were being breached by the BH army? Was that one of his claims?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And for an area to be considered a safe area, wasn't it necessary for this area to clear from all troops, weapons, and other things in order for them to be proper safe areas? Wasn't that the essence of the Security Council resolution and decision, was it not the essence of demilitarisation which was then followed by the establishment of a safe area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I don't think that was the essence or the actual words of the Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to argue with you. I only believe that if something is to be considered a safe area, all and any weapons should be removed from it in order for it to be a real safe area, and it especially must not be abused to launch any military actions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That may be, but that isn't what, in practice, those safe areas were. And, as I say, I don't think the Security Council resolution fits that last sentence -- or penultimate sentence, I'm sorry, in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to General Nicolai, every boy in Sarajevo had a pistol, and there were between 50 and 60.000 men under arms in Sarajevo throughout the whole period relevant for the indictment against General Milosevic. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. And I don't think -- and I wouldn't agree with the assertion that every boy had a pistol or that there were that number of armed men inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm talking solely about the period relevant for the indictment and the liability of General Milosevic for the incidents in and around Sarajevo. But you say that this was not the situation as I described it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: You told me that General Nicolai had said something. I don't agree with what you said General Nicolai said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 9 of the record of your meeting with Karadzic: "Bosnian Serb counter-offensive: Karadzic was at pains to point out the decision had been taken to start a counter-offensive. General Smith probed Karadzic on the form that offensive would take." Was that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I was very interested to know what he was going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Karadzic reply to you by saying that there will be a counter-attack only if they were attacked; otherwise, they would not mount any offensive unless they were attacked? Was that -- was that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: What it says there is they would counter-attack where they have been attacked. It wasn't -- it was about the location, not if.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned here that the preparations for the BH army offensive were under way and that it was mounted on the 5th of June, 1995, as far as Sarajevo was concerned. Is it true that they mounted this offensive?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian side responded to this offensive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 59 of your statement, you say that you met General Delic in Zenica on the 24th of May; then you said it was a useful meeting to gain an insight into Delic's views on the military situation and to get a feel for his military intentions. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Delic tell you at the time that they had been already preparing this offensive, that there was -- nothing that will come out of any peaceful agreement, and that they already had military intention?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The -- the detail of his -- I don't remember how much he told me as to their preparations and to some extent I already, as you've heard, had observed them; and not so -- not for the attack in specifically an attack in Sarajevo, but the general opening up of the offensive and we'd seen this as early as March. I'm sorry. I forgot you asked two questions then and I've forgotten the second one. Oh, yes. It was whether he had come out of any peace -- yes. I don't think -- again, my memory is that he didn't -- it wasn't so much that nothing would come out of negotiation. It was that the -- his business was only the military. It wasn't his business to do negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 60, you talk about the following: "At this stage, the Bosnian Serbs shelled Sarajevo on a regular basis with up to three missions conducted per day. The principal targets areas were the old town, the Jewish cemetery, the PTT building, and the Bosnian army barracks opposite Tito barracks and the area between the Residency and the UN barracks at Zetra stadium. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But then you added the following: "The provocation was not always obvious, but it was clear that the Bosnian army were shelling Serb positions from within the city on a regular basis." Was this also true?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if we're talking about provocations, that means that BH army opened fire first and then the Serbs would respond with three missions a day?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The -- I think we should understand that as two answers to possibly two questions. It doesn't follow that every incident is a result of the provocation. I -- I'm not suggesting there, I don't think, from when I gave that statement that -- or answered that question that the only cause of the shelling by Bosnian Serbs was a provocation by the Bosnians on the inside, or vice versa, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I paid particular attention to the words you used in this part of your statement whereby you said that: "They regularly shelled Serb positions." Can you explain to me what this "regular shelling" actually means in your words.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I think I meant - again when I said that - this was occurring sufficiently that -- often that one could expect it to be happening during that period. Whether this meant two a day, one a day, I don't know, and I suspect that's why in the subsequent sentence I'm saying that they -- you know, if you want the details we'll have to go to the reports of the sector and the situation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 61, well, there we come to a very important problem. You say that: "On the 24th of May, fighting flared again in the Sarajevo area." When you say "fighting," does that mean that there were actions on both sides?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, do you know anything at all about the victims of the bombardment concerning Sarajevo on the Serb side among their soldiers and civilians? Or perhaps you did not have any proper information on that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, we did have information. I don't remember it now, I don't have it to my hand, but we did have an understanding of what was going on both sides of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next sentence of paragraph 61 you say: "The BSA removed weapons from the weapon collection points and failed to return them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on by saying: "I issued an ultimatum to re-establish those." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yeah, to re-establish the exclusion zones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say: "This was ignored and on the 25th of May NATO bombed the Pale ammunition depot." My question is this: Although we cannot see from this that the Serb side did anything other than moving their weapons outside the exclusion zone, they were immediately punished by the bombing of Pale by NATO aircraft. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, because they had not put them back again, which is what they had been told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Couldn't you have waited to see what will happen, because if there was fighting again, it is naturally then one contemplates a military action in order to protect themselves from what may be coming their way.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I didn't and couldn't have waited. I had given my ultimatum and they didn't do what I said they were to do, and so the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What were weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In -- we have to go back about a year into -- sometime in the early part of 1994. The -- the into the no-fly zones had been established, but this was -- there was still attacks into the safe areas using heavy weapons and various exclusion zones were declared around the safe areas and from which all heavy weapons were to be withdrawn into weapon collection points, where they were to be monitored by UN forces. If they left the weapon collection point, then the -- there was an injunction that you called in NATO in response to that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the 24th passed, or rather, the 25th, the very next day you again shelled the positions of the BSA, again at Pale, although something occurred in the meantime in Tuzla, but right away you went on to bomb Pale yet again. Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. There's -- the ultimatum had still not been obeyed and, again at my request, NATO bombed a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The very same day, when the thing in Tuzla happened; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. It was the -- in the following day. If my memory is correct, the shelling of all the safe areas, not only Tuzla, occurred on the evening of the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a shell --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I've got my days one whole day out. It's the 25th that the bombing was on. My memory is it was the evening of the 25th that the Tuzla and the safe areas are shelled and the second lot of bombing is on the 26th. My apologies. I was a day -- a day wrong in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What the actual situation included with a single shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In Tuzla, you mean? It was a single shell that did the killing, as I remember it. It was -- there was more than one in the cell there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, claims were made that that shell hit Tuzla but the problem was the actual distance. What was claimed -- what was that -- the distance was that of several hundred kilometres. What you can tell us about the actual distance that the shell had been fired at Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: 700 kilometres from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance that the shell came from killing those innocent people?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't know, but it isn't 700 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the transcript is erroneous. I said "several," not "700."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But what was the figure, because according to the information I have, there was quite a distance from the place where that shell was fired to the place where it actually landed, killing people?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't know the distance it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And immediately you ordered NATO air-strikes, which were implemented and Pale was bombed, even in its residential quarter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't -- the second air-strike was not a consequence of the attack on Tuzla; however much, that was an attack on a safe area. The attack on the -- the second bombing at Pale was a continuation of the previous engagement on the basis of the ultimatum over the weapon collection points, first of all. And secondly, we did not attack the residential quarters of Pale. We were attacking the ammunition depot outside Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll return to that when we discuss some subsequent NATO bombings, but let us move on to paragraph 71 of your statement which speaks about the offensive that was initiated on the 16th of June. You can see there that you said that that offensive began on that particular day and that there were some initial successes on the part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were quickly thrown back with heavy casualties first and foremost among their soldiers, both at the front lines and in the rear, or rather, closer to the separation lines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just let me ... I'm not quite sure what -- "both at the front lines and in the rear, or rather, closer to the separation..." I'm not sure what that means. I haven't put -- it's not in my statement. You've added that on, and I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my question, in fact. You said that after some initial successes they were quickly thrown back with heavy casualties. My question is this: Were those heavy casualties present at all front lines where the Bosnian Serb forces were, and those casualties were mainly soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The casualties that I'm referring to there were in the attacking force, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a document here, an UNPROFOR document. It is a report by David Harland dated the 24th of June. It is a 65 ter number 2471. This is P16. Perhaps we could have a look so that I can put two things from it to you. I believe it is already up on the screen. It says in paragraph 3: "Last Friday and Saturday," and Harland was reporting this to some other people. It is page 2, paragraph 3. It says: "Last Friday and Saturday (15th, 16th June) Bosnian troops attacked Serb positions all along the confrontation line. Attacking out of the city and into it from the south, west, and north." Was this really so and have you seen this report previously?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I haven't. If I remember correctly, this -- Harland is in Sector Sarajevo at the time, so his reports as such would not cross my desk as a matter of course. But that paragraph 3 that you're directing my attention to, it is as I remember the events at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to hear. Let's look at the next paragraph T provided a -- I translated it to myself correctly. "After a day or two, the Bosniaks subsequently broke off their attacks apparently because of the heavy casualties sustained in the initial assaults. UNPROFOR is unable to make an accurate estimate of these casualties, however, as the Bosnians no longer allow UNPROFOR free access to the sector's hospitals." Would you agree with what is stated here, that UNPROFOR had no access to the hospital so as to be able to establish who the victims of the showdown were.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's a showdown, but I don't recall the business with the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if -- that is in Harland's report, that being an official report. Then I believe we can safely presume that Harland described the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: So can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object. The -- counsel put it to the witness, he said what he could say about it, and now counsel is testifying about what he thinks about the document. So I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this has been admitted in any case. Let us go to paragraph 99: "The rest of July and the first part of August were dominated by the combined HV, Croatia army and HVO, offensive in Livno, Glamoc, Grahovo, and the HV offensives into the Krajinas." Was that so.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 100, you say: "I had a meeting with General Mladic on 31st July at Mrkonjic Grad." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to 101 then: "The first part of the meeting was dominated by Mladic's description of the military and humanitarian situation in western Bosnia, as a result of the HV and HOV offensives." Is that so.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Mladic was obviously very concerned about the military situation and appeared tired and harassed. He appealed to me to carry a message to the Security Council to demand an immediate end to the attacks and the withdrawal of the Croatians from Bosnian-held territory." Was that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what is the relevance of all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he continues by saying, "I shared Mladic' concerns about the situation as it was quite clear that fighting would spread; however, I pointed out that the HV offensive could be justified by Article 51 of the UN charter." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, my question is this: The Croatian army coming from another state into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina across the century-long Serb territories and when fire is opened on all sides, you still find it in the spirit of Article 51 of the Charter, and you find it justified that one state enters another and that they say that they have the right to do that since it was their right to defend themselves. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I said it could be, as opposed to it was. And I would have to go back and review the actual situation as to what each contingent was doing as to exactly why I said that, because I cannot remember at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you at least confirm that the Serbian people in the territories where they had been living for centuries had the right to defend themselves under the UN Charter. If the Croats had the right to cross somebody else's territory, did the Serbs also have the right to defend their own homes and their own people, their brothers and sisters?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Is your question related to the Croatian Serbs in the Krajinas?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My question relates to the Serbs living in an and Sarajevo, in that area, where this armed conflict was in progress. Did they have the right to defend themselves in the spirit of Article 51 of the UN Charter, if Croatia was allowed to cross somebody else's territory and defend itself in that manner?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: My answer is I don't know, because I can't remember why I said that point about Article 51 of the Charter. And I would need to know the situation on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in these attacks in particular to understand the situation again, to make a proper answer for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, let me ask you about two incidents that happened in June and July. According to the documents that I have with me - actually, these are UNPROFOR reports - did you know that on the 18th of June, the former school was hit. The school was called Simone Bolivar - I find it difficult to remember this name, although I know who Simone Bolivar was - and that there were civilian casualties, people who died there. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Where was the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was impossible to establish who fired this shell, whether it was the Serbs or the Muslims? Do you remember this incident or maybe you were not in Sarajevo at all at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I think I probably was in June, and I don't remember the incident, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this incident? It was -- it received wide coverage in the press worldwide, especially in Sarajevo, and I'm referring now to the incident of the 28th of June when the TV building was hit. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Again, not specifically, no, I don't. That was the TV building in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you don't remember this incident, because it's been a long time - It was ten years ago - or is it because there were was so many incidents of the same nature that it's difficult to remember just this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably a bit of both. Also, the -- remember, I'm commanding more than just Sarajevo. I'm in Sarajevo, but I have other responsibilities; and at that particular time, in my memory, I'm very concerned about re-supplying the eastern enclaves, who have not been supplied with humanitarian aid since sometime in March and April. So I suspect my complete focus was somewhere other than Sarajevo at that time, in addition to there were lots of incidents that covered the whole of my command, and it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General Smith, sir, is it possible that your command never received an UNPROFOR report - and this is something to be the subject of deliberation by this Court when establishing the truth - that the following day, the building of the Bosnia-Herzegovina television was hit by the -- a shell fired by BH army? Is it possible that your command did not receive this kind of information? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: If this incident occurred, there would have been a report. It -- not all reports come to me. Even if I'm in the headquarters, there is a system for filtering them out and aggregating them out and so forth. That incident, as reported, I'm sure occurred. Whether they were drawn to my attention is another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would that have surprised you if that did in fact take place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if that had occurred, it would have been brought to my attention at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Would it have surprised you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That the television building had been hit by a shell fired by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And as I say, I think it would have been brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, Mr. Nicolai, that is the person in charge of your General Staff, wrote a letter on the 1st of July, 1995 addressed to Ratko Mladic. That's 65 ter 02498, P103. This is it. And it roads as follows: "I write to you to protest most strongly about the recent and indiscriminate and deliberate shelling of the residence parts of the city of Sarajevo." In paragraph 3, he says,"I hereby send you a copy of the letter of protest from acting commander Sector Sarajevo Colonel Robert May to Major-General Milosevic commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps regarding the incidents of the 28th and 29th June, 1995." Do you remember these two letters; first, the one to Milosevic and the second one to Ratko Mladic? Was this produced by your staff and members of your staff? Is it possible that you don't remember this either?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this. And I should add on the 1st of July, I went on leave, so I probably wasn't there when this was sent. But it is -- I have no doubt that this -- these letters were written, and it indicates the point I was making earlier. I commanded more than Sector Sarajevo. Sector Sarajevo was the primary headquarters dealing with the local forces; the corps, in this case of General Milosevic. And my Chief of Staff would be permitted by me to act in this way, particularly in my absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: If these two letters were written on the 1st of July and the second one on the same date; that is, on the 30th of June which is two days after the incident, what could General Mladic, and General Milosevic deduce about this incidents, if even the 29th of June, UNPROFOR claimed that it was something that had been done by the BH army? How were they supposed to establish who of their soldiers was responsible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Because he is not in a position to say what they would have deduced. So please ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to ask him anything further. I think that this has been recorded in the transcript, and I don't believe that I need to offer any further explanations, as I also believe the General Smith is not able to answer this. You are absolutely right. I cannot rephrase my question now, given that General Smith was absent on that day. In any case, it will be up to you, Your Honours, to resolve this issue because up to this date we still don't know who committed these acts. And I'm sure that General Smith is not the person to answer this question because it was an impossible request if somebody else did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, just get on with the questioning and stop making speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do that very seldom, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me refer you to one more report, General. It's dated the 2nd of July, 1995, 65 ter 2503, Exhibit P19, page 3 of the English version. Page 3 of the English version: "Location of Bosnian weapons a problem." It roads as follows: "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago..." So the first question would be: You said a few days; whereas, Harland's report says that the offensive started two weeks ago, and it doesn't specific when it ended. Therefore, did the offensive end after three days, or was it ongoing for two weeks already as it says here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Who wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This report was compiled by David Harland from civilian affairs, and it is addressed to Philip Corwin.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, that's all right. So it's coming out as Sector Sarajevo; that's really my point. If Harland wrote the report and in a previous one he has said that the attack petered out after a couple of days, in the paragraph you've put here, a subsequent report, and he is clearly only referencing the start of the attack, not -- not suggesting that it is continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What he says is that this attack has been going on for two weeks , but thank you for your answer. You did your best. He went on to say --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I don't think he say that at all. He says: "Since the attack." It doesn't say it's been going on all that time. If I could have that page back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Since the Bosnian offensive began two weeks ago." It doesn't say that it ended any time.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, but in a previous report by the same man, he says it only lasted two days after it started. So we might deduce that he's only using the words "since the Bosnian offensive started two weeks ago," in other words two -- he could have said on the - whatever the date was - 16th, the number of -- you know, he could have written since the 16th of June, the number of Bosnian heavy weapons, blah, blah, blah, but that's all he's saying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are the only one who was claimed in your testimony that this offensive lasted for two or three days. No one else said that, and there's a difference between that and what is written in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to make up our minds about that. We have heard the witness's evidence and we have your submissions as to what it means. We'll have to draw our conclusions, so please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The report goes on to say that: "The number of Bosnian heavy weapons operated from near UNPROFOR facilities has significantly increased. Some people in UNPROFOR see this as an effort by the Bosnians to draw counter-battery fire on to UNPROFOR, which would then be drawn into conflicts with the Serbs." Does this correspond to the factual situation, what is written in the report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: You must read the whole paragraph that's also in front of me, and you say that others note that there is a general increase, et cetera, et cetera. And that is the same answer that I gave you earlier when you talked about mobile weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I'm going to insist upon and that is as follows. "Others note that there has been a general increase in the number of active weapons and that the density of heavy weapons is not great around UNPROFOR facilitates than it is elsewhere." Is it true that these heavy weapons were not only deployed there but in all other locations in the area of responsibility of the BH army? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: The point is that there was an increase because they brought in extra people from outside, through the tunnel, as we've discussed, and there was an increase of Bosnian forces inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There was an increase in the number of heavy pieces in Sarajevo. Can we say that? That's what I conclude from this report.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Not -- not heavy weapons as -- in the exclusion zone, those that were banned in the exclusion zone. We're talking about the lighter mortars and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't even begun asking questions about Markale, and however I needed to go through these documents, this one in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your judgement as to what is important to your case must be questioned. You have three hours. You have five minutes left for the three hours and you haven't done Markale? You have been going through these -- all these statements to what purpose, I don't know. I am told that we can't be here beyond 5.20, and it was not my intention to give you more than three hours. Move on to Markale immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. But I will to ask all these questions in order to sketch a picture of General Smith's position and feelings and how he was prone to order the bombardment of Serb positions before I got to Markale. I thought it was impossible for me to deal with Markale without providing that picture for you first; and if you deem Markale to be unimportant, then I will stop, but I don't think that will be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have told you to move on to it, so move on to it and stop talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I have to put two documents to you in order to try to clarify something, although I might not have the time needed. The first one is drafted by Konings -- excuse me, by Lieutenant Higgs who was one of Konings team members. It is 65 ter number 198.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The parole leader was Konings, and the members were Lieutenant Higgs and Captain Karbone [phoen], the general part. It says here on the first page: "The investigation team carried out the entire investigation as a group, excluding the visit to -- including the hospital so as to confirm the number of casualties, or rather, of those killed and injured." And there was an investigation team from the Ministry of the Interior, then there were their observations. "The parole investigated five impact sites, all of which were from 122-millimetre mortar projectiles. One projectile was fired from the 70-degrees azimuth and killed 33 people and wounded 58 in a busy market area," and then a part of the second sentence is illegible. In item 2: "The bearings in combination with the estimated angle of impact could give no evidence of the origin of fire, since it is not known with which charge the projectile has been fired." And not to have to read the whole thing, I will move on to page 2. "In cooperation with the investigation team of the Ministry of the Interior, this team was able to confirm that 38 were killed and 64 wounded. We were unable to show" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading since the interpreters cannot see that page on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters are complaining that you're reading too fast. Just put your question now. What is the question for the witness, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The UNPROFOR investigation team confirmed that it cannot be established -- that the origin of fire cannot be established since they were unable to discern what the type of projectile was." Have you ever seen this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I haven't seen that specific one, no. But have I seen the subsequent one, and it isn't an UNPROFOR report; it is an UNMO report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a report sent by General Janvier to the UN directly to Mr. Annan, Secretary-General, on that same day?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Probably, but I don't recall it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It tallies completely with that previous report, and in that document at page DD000-10. UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo, in the English page 3. So as not to have to read the whole thing, I just wanted to tell you that the contents resemble very much the previous report, saying that: "It is very difficult to determine the exact place of firing in the case of mortar rounds because it is impossible to establish what the type and amount of charge was." It has to do with the 28th of August. Due to such characteristics of the shell, it was unable to establish the things mentioned here. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. This is my superior headquarters routine situation report, as I understand it, made up of aggregating together the subordinate reports coming up to them so they would have -- if they had the UNMO report available to them, they would have used and sending it on to UN headquarters in New York. That's what I understood from the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Colonel Demurenko, the Russian colonel, said when he came to the spot among the first people to be there? I asked one of the witnesses about that, but do you know what Demurenko said? I think he said something along the lines that, It is impossible that those shells came from the positions of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I remember him saying that, but not immediately after the event. It was some two days, 36 hours after the event or maybe a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you stopped NATO air-strikes for a day?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I -- I didn't stop them for a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did they stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We stopped them - and this was not a decision of mine by that stage - after about five to seven days of action for a period of about -- if my memory is -- about four days. If that's what we're referring to, then I was party to that decision. But it wasn't strictly mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, was that what you were referring to, or were you referring to the -- when you asked whether the General had stopped NATO air-strikes, did you mean immediately after Markale?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, a few days later, once it became public what Demurenko said. I ask that we look at page 730, line 17. I asked the witness Mohatarem the following: "On the 1st of September, the bombing stopped because of Colonel Demurenko's claims that the shelling was not done by the BSA." And I asked the witness whether it was correct. He answered: "It is." Therefore, on the 1st of September, the next day after the bombing, once Demurenko's opinion became public, the bombing was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It was not suspended because of anything that Colonel Demurenko said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know why it was suspended, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is covered in paragraph 113 of my statement. The reason for it was so that the Force Commander, General Janvier, could meet with General Mladic and to see whether the demanded that we had laid upon the Bosnian Serbs as part of this bombing, which involved the withdrawal of all heavy weapons outside the exclusion zone, would be met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see that, Mr. Tapuskovic? It's in paragraph 113 of the General' statement: "On the 1st September, a 24-hour pause was agreed to while the force commander met Mladic in the morning." Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1023, page 16 to 25 of the transcript, that's why General Nicolai says: "Yes, the Dutch radars," and he also mentioned the British ones, "did not register the shell which caused so many people to be killed and injured." Were you told this that the radars did not register that event? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: 1027, page 19 to 22, Nicolai again: "The only thing I can say is it wasn't registered by any radars. That's why we had to analyse the craters in the ground." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: That isn't so, in quite that way that you have expressed that sentence. We analysed the craters in the ground in any event. We, as you see from the UNMO report, that was one of the things they did immediately you had such an incident. We then would gather all other information that was available to us; and in this case, that included finding out what the radars had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this piece of information reached you. It's on page 1028, lines 4 to 23. It refers to a report that a shell hit a building and caused the shell to explode in the air. That is what Mr. Nicolai said before this Chamber. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I didn't know he'd said that, no. Or are you referring to the-- to the shell exploding in the air?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicolai claimed that he had received a report that a shell hit the roof of building and then disintegrated hitting people on the street?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: He may have received such a report, but it is evidently a wrong report because there were five craters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 1039, lines 7 to 10. I asked General Nicolai the following: "Does this fit with what you were told by Mr. Van Baal that when it comes to the highest -- state interest, one would sacrifice ones own people?" And Nicolai replied, "We did not rule out this option." I'm asking you were you aware of this option? Was your staff aware of this option or not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: In a theoretical fashion, and if I'm to understand you to say that the option is that this was an act inflicted by the Bosnians on the Bosnians, then theoretically that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, nonetheless, that evening you issued an order for air-strikes on the Bosnian Serb army positions. In spite of all these ambiguities, incomplete investigation, you issued, as you said if your statement, an order that evening for the air-strikes to again.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: It wasn't like that precisely. First of all, there were other investigations going on by Sector Sarajevo and my own staff. Secondly, the -- there were two people required to make this decision. In the jargon of the day, there were two keys to turn. I held one key at the time and the other was held by Admiral Leighton Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two more things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, explain to me again what your case is on this point; that is, the NATO having air-strikes on Bosnian Serb army positions even before the investigation was completed. Explain again how your case is built up on that. I believe it has something to do with the argument you make that there was collaboration between NATO and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I skipped so many things. In paragraph 113 of the witness's statement, he says as follows: "Attacks were carried out to achieve air supremacy to show the extent and nature of the punishment to come and to destroy weapons, command and control, and weapon dumps." If you look carefully at this paragraph, you will see that they sided with the BH army. There was an incident which was not properly investigated. These are the words of General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this what you said? "The punishment to come and to destroy weapons, command and control, and weapons dumps."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Are you asking me that I said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the objective?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Those were the objectives of that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you mainly struck military targets, but also the entire infrastructure of the positions and places where Serbs were living in the environs of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No, it's not. We only attacked military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, is your case that Markale was caused by a BH attack? No, just answer me. Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And is it also your case that NATO was complicit in that attack, or that NATO would have known about the BH army attacking the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And let me conclude my examination with what I began. The witness knows, and I will put it to him directly - it's something that I found in Alija Izetbegovic's book - that on the 29th, he had a meeting in the US Embassy in Paris with Holbrooke, and that he also talked to Talbot, Christopher's deputy, and that he had been told that the attacks against the Serbian forces would start promptly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it where the order calm from?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. The decision lay in equal shares between the two key holders; that was Admiral Smith and me. And it stems from the London Conference of July, late in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question will be as follows: Is it true what Alija Izetbegovic claims in his book, that this was a concerted action all together, in the sense that I have just put it to, that he went to Paris precisely with this intention, and that this was all coordinated at this level?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no questions, thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, time is it running out, but I would wish to put a just few final questions to relating to the accused's involvement in these matters. So my first question would be: Did you ever meet with General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: I met with him, if my memory is correct, only after the end of the bombing in September. And I think we had two, possibly no more, meetings. And it was all to go through and explain what was required of him and his corps as a result of the consequence of the bombings taking place and an agreement being reached with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Milosevic comply with the agreements that you made with him during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: More or less. I think the first time this occurred, there was some back sliding or failure to comply. But the -- the trend was positive, and it got more positive as the days went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have other sorts of communication with General Milosevic? Not physically present, one in face of the other, but by communication, by letters, by mails, or by instructions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: This would be done at Sector Sarajevo level. So in the sense of this was my subordinates communicating with him, yes, but directly, I don't remember a direct communication either by letter or -- or face to face, other than those that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you, during your term in office, at any point, made aware of General Milosevic being unable to comply with the terms of the agreements that were entered into either by you or other UN agencies on the one hand and the Serb leadership on the other?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: Being unable to comply because he was ordered not to or because there was some physical barrier to prevent him from complying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Just wait for the translation. My question relates to his inability to control the forces under his command.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH.
utterances.text: No. I have no evidence of that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, General, that concludes your testimony. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. I also wish to thank the interpreters and the other officers of the court for their extraordinary service, which is consistent with the best traditions of international civil service. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
